These are player-use explanations, not new automatic bonuses. Skill Usual Ability What It Lets You Attempt Acrobatics DEX Balance, controlled movement, tumbling, landing and physically awkward agility. Animal Handling WIS Calm, understand, direct or manage ordinary trainable creatures. Arcana INT Magic, Aether theory, magical phenomena, spell structures and intellectual Aether analysis. Athletics STR Climb, jump, swim, grapple-related exertion and other raw physical effort. Deception CHA Mislead, bluff, conceal intent, maintain a false story or impersonate. History INT Recall public history, cultures, institutions, conflicts and notable people or places. Insight WIS Read motives, sincerity, emotional state and social intent; not mind reading. Intimidation CHA Pressure, threaten or project authority when coercion is plausible. Investigation INT Reason from clues, search methodically, understand mechanisms and reconstruct events. Medicine WIS Stabilize a dying creature, diagnose injuries/afflictions and administer relevant care. Nature INT Terrain, plants, ordinary wildlife, ecosystems, weather and natural hazards. Perception WIS Notice creatures, ambushes, sounds, traps, hidden details and immediate sensory changes. Performance CHA Sing, act, dance, entertain or sustain a deliberate artistic performance. Persuasion CHA Negotiate, appeal, request cooperation or change a position when plausible. Religion INT Doctrines, rites, religious history, sacred customs and spiritual traditions. Sleight of Hand DEX Precise manual manipulation, theft, mechanisms and physical Aether interaction when called for. Stealth DEX Hide, move quietly, remain unnoticed or maintain concealment. Survival WIS Track, navigate, read wilderness signs, avoid becoming lost and manage wilderness operations. Proficiency vs. Expertise. Proficiency adds PB once. Expertise doubles the PB contribution for one proficient Skill. A duplicate proficiency never becomes Expertise automatically.

text: Acolyte What Is an Acolyte?. An Acolyte has meaningful experience with religious or spiritual service, sacred traditions, temples, ceremonies, or communities of worship. Life and Origins. The character may have been raised around a temple, studied under a religious teacher, volunteered in a sacred institution, maintained holy places, assisted ceremonies, or found faith after a life-changing event. Motivations and Outlook. Faith, service, protection, reform, doubt, duty, spiritual curiosity, or concern for a community may lead an Acolyte into adventure. An Acolyte can be devout, questioning, disillusioned, or seeking a new understanding. Playing an Acolyte. Decide what teachings shaped you and what relationship you have with them now. The Background does not require the Cleric or Chanter Class and does not automatically grant divine magic.

text: Acquisition Weapons, armor, shields, and implements are not normally sold by ordinary merchants. They enter play through starting equipment, faction issue, exploration, battlefield loot, caches, armories, relic sites, defeated enemies who actually possess them, quest rewards, and major adventures. What to Do Every Time You Level Up • Read the full class-level entry and every specialization feature gained at that level. • Increase maximum HP using the class's fixed HP gain, CON modifier and class durability rules. • Update PB only if the universal table changes it. • Update class resource caps, dice, ranges, trap limits, spirit/Bastion chassis or other scaling. • Make an ASI/Feat choice if the level grants one. • Apply Spell Advancements if your class grants them, using the spell advancement rules. • Update Flight Slots, Exploration Flight and Inventory Slots. • Recalculate class Save DC, spell attack, AC, passive values and PB/ability-dependent features. • If you are changing your Active Profession, make that change now; Active Profession changes are allowed only when you gain a character level. Character Manager. Apply level-up choices and resulting character-state changes in the Wings of Atreia Character Manager after resolving the governing class and advancement rules. The rules determine what changes; the Character Manager records and tracks the resulting character state. title: Aether & Spellcasting
desc: Aether environment and interaction, universal spellcasting, and Spell Advancement.
text: Player Rules Aether & Spellcasting Aether environment and interaction, universal spellcasting, and Spell Advancement. Website rules source: Wings of Atreia Player Handbook v3.10 — Publication Master, 8 September 2026. This page preserves the handbook's player-facing rules and terminology. Aether Environment, Interaction & Gathering Aether Interaction Aether Sources Refined Aether Gathering Aether Hazards Universal Spellcasting Universal Model Spell Acquisition Aether Environment, Interaction & Gathering Aether Interaction Aether Interaction uses Intelligence (Arcana) for intellectual analysis and Dexterity (Sleight of Hand) for physical manipulation. Typical DC guidance is 10, 12, 15, 18, or 20+ according to complexity and danger. Aether Sources Nodes, Currents, Fissures, and other environmental Aether phenomena can provide opportunities, hazards, travel effects, or Refined Aether. Their exact scene behavior is defined by the source. Refined Aether Gathering Gathering Refined Aether uses Dexterity (Sleight of Hand) against the source DC. Aether Level DC Yield Range Default Yield 1 8 2–6 4 2 10 6–12 9 3 12 12–24 18 4 15 24–40 32 5 18 40–60 50 The GM identifies a valid source and its Aether Level. Only the interacting character rolls. Apply normal modifiers and Help only if actually meaningful. On success, gain a yield within the listed range based on source richness; if no special richness is established, use the Default Yield. A successful gathering normally exhausts that source. Multiple deposits exist only when the GM explicitly establishes them. Failure gives no Refined Aether and does not automatically exhaust the source, but a new attempt requires a meaningful change in circumstances. Another party member does not automatically create a fresh attempt. Normal gathering is not performed during active combat unless gathering itself is an explicit encounter objective. Already-refined Aether recovered from caches or stores is ordinary loot and requires no gathering check. Aether Hazards Aether Hazards use the universal sequence Trigger → Save → DC → Effect → Duration. Standard severity bands are Minor DC 10–11, Moderate DC 12–14, Severe DC 15–17, and Extreme DC 18–20+. The four approved hazard families are Aether Storm, Aether Surge, Aether Eruption, and Unstable Zone. Each specific hazard defines its actual Trigger, Save, Effect, and Duration. Dangerous Aether changes are normally telegraphed in advance unless the hazard is specifically concealed. Strategic Refined Aether uses not defined in this handbook are deferred unless a future subsystem explicitly establishes them. Vehicle-related Refined Aether rules remain deferred with vehicle rules, and the current Abyss Warfront system uses no universal Refined Aether conversion for Fortress power. Universal Spellcasting Universal Model WoA has no spell slots and no cantrip category. Each spell is individually At-Will, Cooldown-based, Short-Rest limited, or Long-Rest limited. Class resources may modify spells but are not universal casting costs. Spell Acquisition Spells are class-granted abilities. They cannot be bought, sold, looted, copied from spellbooks or scrolls, learned from vendors, or acquired by commerce or exploration. A spell becomes available only when the character reaches its Unlock Level and, when applicable, satisfies the immediately preceding spell in its linear prerequisite chain. Unlocking a later spell never removes the earlier spell. Newly unlocked spells begin at Spell Level 1 unless explicitly stated otherwise. Spell Advancement — Final Rule. A class grants Spell Advancements according to its finalized progression. One Spell Advancement raises one eligible unlocked spell by 1 Spell Level, subject to that class’s Maximum Spell Level and listed prerequisites. Unspent Spell Advancements may be banked indefinitely, but banked or newly earned Spell Advancements may be spent only when the character gains a level; they cannot normally be spent during an adventure, between encounters, or during a rest. A character cannot spend more Spell Advancements than they have earned. Spell Retraining. There is no universal spell retraining. Once a Spell Advancement is spent, it is permanent unless a specific class feature, explicit story effect, or GM-approved exceptional circumstance directly permits reassignment. Casting Frequency and Action Economy At-Will spells may be cast whenever action economy permits. Cooldown X spells become available at the start of the caster’s Xth turn after the casting turn. Round-based cooldowns advance only during genuine combat; artificial Initiative cannot refresh, farm, or manipulate cooldowns or class resources. Outside genuine combat, a Cooldown spell becomes available again 1 minute after use unless the spell states a longer restriction. Short-Rest and Long-Rest spells regain uses after the named rest. Casting Time is binding. Casting multiple spells in one turn is allowed only when the character actually has the required Actions and no class or spell restriction forbids it. title: Aethertech
desc: Complete player reference for the Aethertech class in Wings of Atreia, based on Player Handbook v3.10.
text: Bastion Pilot • Aether Core • Heat • Adaptive Weapons Combat Aethertech “Steel, meet face. Face, meet steel.” Website rules source: Wings of Atreia Player Handbook v3.10 — Publication Master, 8 September 2026. This page preserves the handbook's class material and ordering. Class Identity Class Chassis Resource Flow — Generation, Recovery, Spending & Reset Specializations Preview Level 1–20 Action & Resource Reference Level-by-Level Progression Example System Sequence Tradition & Outlook Appearance & Adventuring Specialization Reassignment The Aethertech fights from one piloted Medium Bastion platform. The pilot and Bastion are one character’s action economy, not two independent turns. The class alternates between integrated Bastion armaments, Aether Core expenditures, controlled Heat accumulation, venting, repairs, and system integration. The Bastion is a separate physical HP pool that enemies can damage without directly healing or harming the pilot unless an effect specifically targets the pilot. Class Identity Aethertechs are technist warriors who channel Aether through a Bastion: a magical-mechanical combat platform that transforms how the Daeva occupies the battlefield. The class combines personal skill, engineered systems, heavy protection, and controlled bursts of power. Aether Core and Heat represent the constant balance between available energy and the strain created by pushing the Bastion harder. Tradition & Outlook Aethertech is a comparatively modern Daeva discipline born from the recovery, study, and weaponization of advanced magical technology. The wider Aion tradition connects the class to Daeva analysis of Danuar technology and the lessons surrounding Hyperion; Wings of Atreia preserves that technological identity while its own campaign chronology and mechanics remain authoritative. Aethertechs often value ingenuity, technical discipline, experimentation, and the belief that knowledge taken from dangerous enemies can be turned toward Atreia’s defense. Appearance & Adventuring An Aethertech is visually defined by the Bastion and the contrast between a Daeva operator and an imposing Aether-powered war platform. Outside it, the Aethertech remains a trained combatant using the class’s approved weapons and equipment. Aethertechs adventure to recover technology, test designs under real conditions, oppose Balaur war machines, protect expeditions with a durable mobile platform, or prove that engineering can stand beside sword and spell as a heroic discipline. Class Chassis Trait Rule Primary Ability Intelligence Secondary Ability Constitution Hit Die d8 Saving Throws Intelligence, Constitution Armor Chain Armor Weapons Shortswords, Maces, Hammers Signature Resources Aether Core and Heat Signature Mechanic Piloted Bastion Class Save DC 8 + PB + INT modifier Extra Attack Level 5; two Bastion weapon attacks only Spellcasting None Bastion Targeting and Chassis The pilot and Bastion have separate HP and temporary HP. Repairs restore Bastion HP and are not healing. While occupied, ordinary physical attacks targeting the Aethertech generally strike the Bastion first. Mental, emotional, biological, and similar effects target the pilot when appropriate. One area effect normally does not double-hit both pilot and Bastion. Bastion physical STR/DEX/CON saves use PB + INT modifier. Mental saves use the pilot’s relevant save. When the Bastion reaches 0 HP it is Disabled. The pilot is ejected to the nearest legal space, takes 1d6 Force damage, and does not provoke Opportunity Attacks from the ejection. A disabled Bastion retains its current Core and Heat; a fresh chassis does not replace it. A Short Rest repairs a Disabled or damaged Bastion to half its maximum HP, if it currently has less HP than that amount. A Long Rest repairs the Bastion to its maximum HP. These restorations are repairs, not healing. Once the Bastion has at least 1 HP, it is operational. Entering or re-entering a deployed Bastion uses an Action when otherwise legal. A defeated or voluntarily replaced Bastion never functions as a companion or second PC. Level Band Bastion AC Bastion Maximum HP 1–4 11 + PB 8 + (5 × Aethertech level) + INT 5–10 12 + PB 8 + (5 × level) + INT 11–17 13 + PB 12 + (6 × level) + INT 18–20 13 + PB 16 + (7 × level) + INT Whenever a chassis improvement raises maximum HP, increase current Bastion HP by the same amount; this is a maximum-HP adjustment rather than healing. Bastion Weapon Synchronization While piloting a Bastion, designate one eligible carried weapon with which you are proficient as your Synchronized Weapon. A Bastion weapon attack roll is 1d20 + PB + INT modifier + the Synchronized Weapon's current equipment-quality bonus to Hit. Only that quality bonus transfers. The Bastion does not inherit the carried weapon's damage dice, damage type, properties, Critical Edge, reload mechanics, critical effects, or other traits. Only one Synchronized Weapon applies at a time; bonuses from multiple weapons never stack. Synchronization does not alter Bastion damage or save DCs. Targeting Array remains a separate once-per-turn +1 class-feature bonus and applies normally. Aether Core Maximum Aether Core equals PB + INT modifier, minimum 3; Level 9 increases this maximum by 1. A Long Rest restores all Core and a Short Rest restores PB. Core powers Bastion systems rather than ordinary movement or basic cannon attacks. Core Cycling later rewards making attacks without spending Core on the attack itself. Heat Heat returns to 0 after 1 minute outside genuine combat without intensive Bastion operation and is produced only by systems or features that explicitly say they gain Heat. Heat maximum is 5 at Levels 1–4, 6 at 5–8, 7 at 9–14, 8 at 15–19, and 9 at Level 20. Stable Heat is 0–2. At 3+ Heat the reactor is Pressurized and your Bastion weapon damage gains the class’s Pressurized bonus: +1 early, +2 from Level 9 onward. At maximum Heat you cannot voluntarily activate a system that would generate more Heat unless a feature explicitly permits it. If an allowed effect raises Heat above maximum, resolve that effect and then Overheat. Vent: Bonus Action, reduce Heat by 2. At Level 15 Vent reduces by 3; Cooling Fins increases the amount by 1. Overheat: take 2d6 Force damage to the Bastion, then reset Heat to 3; from Level 15 reset to 4. Your own Emergency Plating cannot reduce Overheat damage. Controlled Critical at Level 9: if you start your turn at maximum Heat, the first Bastion weapon hit that turn adds PB damage. Heat reduction from “preventing Heat gain” is not the same as Venting/cooling for features that care about cooling. text: Altgard Altgard is a settled military frontier where Asmodian communities, roads, defenses, and patrol routes exist in close relationship with contested territory. Unlike the capital, its identity is shaped by the expectation that danger may arrive from beyond the next defended line. Soldiers and civilians share the same landscape, creating a region where preparedness is part of ordinary life. Its settlements demonstrate that a frontier can be both inhabited and militarily important. Archons operating in Altgard can expect patrols, escorts, reconnaissance, local defense, and missions where information about movement is as important as defeating an enemy. Communities should feel practiced in frontier life rather than permanently helpless, while Daevas provide the extraordinary force needed when ordinary defenses are exceeded. The region naturally supports stories about responsibility and the cost of keeping routes open. Altgard makes Asmodae’s military experience visible at the scale of roads, settlements, and watchful borders.

text: Appendix D — Conditions Fourteen universal Conditions: Blinded, Charmed, Deafened, Frightened, Grappled, Incapacitated, Invisible, Paralyzed, Petrified, Poisoned, Prone, Restrained, Stunned, Unconscious. Hidden is not a Condition. Condition Player-Facing Effect Blinded A Blinded creature cannot see and automatically fails Ability Checks that require sight. Attack rolls against it have Advantage, and its attack rolls have Disadvantage. It can still move normally unless another rule limits its movement, and Blinded does not inherently cause an airborne creature to fall. Charmed A Charmed creature cannot willingly attack, damage, or directly target its charmer with a harmful ability or effect. The charmer has Advantage on appropriate social Ability Checks directed at the Charmed creature. Charmed is not total mind control: it does not create automatic obedience, betrayal, disclosure of secrets, or suicidal behavior. Deafened A Deafened creature cannot hear and automatically fails Ability Checks that require hearing. Deafened creates no generic combat penalty by itself, but the creature cannot benefit from an effect that explicitly requires it to hear the source unless that effect says otherwise. Frightened While the source of its fear is within Line of Sight, a Frightened creature has Disadvantage on Ability Checks and attack rolls and cannot willingly move closer to that source. Frightened imposes no general saving-throw penalty. An airborne Frightened creature may remain airborne and may move sideways or away from the source subject to normal flight rules. Grappled A Grappled creature’s Speed becomes 0. The condition ends if the grappler becomes Incapacitated, the target is moved outside the grappler’s reach, or an explicit effect ends the Grapple. The Grappled creature may use its Action to attempt the approved escape contest. Grappled does not inherently cause Prone or falling; airborne movement follows the normal grappling and forced-movement rules. Incapacitated An Incapacitated creature cannot take Actions, Bonus Actions, or Reactions and cannot maintain Concentration. Incapacitated does not itself reduce Speed to 0, cause Prone, or cause an airborne creature to fall. Invisible An Invisible creature cannot normally be seen without a special sense or revealing effect. Attack rolls against it have Disadvantage and its attack rolls have Advantage when the opposing creature cannot otherwise perceive it, subject to the normal unseen-attacker and unseen-target rules. Invisible is not automatically Hidden; sound, footprints, disturbances, and other evidence can still reveal its location. Paralyzed A Paralyzed creature is Incapacitated, its Speed is 0, and it cannot move or speak. It automatically fails Strength and Dexterity saving throws, and attack rolls against it have Advantage. Paralyzed does not cause automatic Critical Hits. If unsupported, the creature becomes Prone; an unsupported airborne Paralyzed creature therefore falls. Petrified A Petrified creature and its carried nonmagical equipment are transformed into inert solid substance. The creature is Incapacitated, its Speed is 0, it is unaware of its surroundings, it automatically fails Strength and Dexterity saving throws, and attack rolls against it have Advantage. It has Resistance to all damage and does not age or require food, water, air, or sleep while Petrified. An airborne Petrified creature becomes Prone and falls. Poisoned A Poisoned creature has Disadvantage on attack rolls and Ability Checks. Poisoned causes no automatic damage unless the effect that imposed it says otherwise. Prone A Prone creature can move only by Crawling unless it stands. Standing from Prone requires a full Action and consumes no movement. Attack rolls against the Prone creature have Advantage when the attacker is within 5 feet and Disadvantage when the attacker is farther than 5 feet. An unsupported airborne creature that becomes Prone immediately falls. Restrained A Restrained creature’s Speed is 0. Attack rolls against it have Advantage, its attack rolls have Disadvantage, and it has Disadvantage on Dexterity saving throws. Restrained does not automatically cause falling; an airborne Daeva hovers while it can otherwise maintain flight and has Flight Slots as required. Stunned A Stunned creature is Incapacitated, its Speed is 0, and it can speak only falteringly. It automatically fails Strength and Dexterity saving throws, and attack rolls against it have Advantage. Stunned does not inherently cause Prone or falling; an airborne Daeva hovers while it can otherwise maintain flight and has Flight Slots as required. Unconscious An Unconscious creature is Incapacitated, its Speed is 0, and it is unaware of its surroundings. It drops unsecured actively held items, automatically fails Strength and Dexterity saving throws, and attack rolls against it have Advantage. It becomes Prone unless physically supported; an unsupported airborne Unconscious creature therefore falls. Unconscious does not cause automatic Critical Hits. When Unconscious because it is Dying at 0 HP, the Dying rules govern damage and Death Saving Throws. Airborne Reminder. Prone is the universal condition that causes an unsupported airborne creature to fall. Unconscious leads to Prone. Other Conditions do not automatically cause falling unless their text creates Prone or explicitly ends flight. Airborne Reminder. text: Artisan What Is an Artisan?. An Artisan is a skilled maker whose life has been shaped by a practical craft. Smiths, armorers, carpenters, tailors, jewelers, cooks, builders, leatherworkers, and many other trades can fit this Background. Life and Origins. Training may come from family, a master, an apprenticeship, a workshop, or independent practice. Artisan life emphasizes patience, precision, materials, tools, workmanship, and the value of making something well. Motivations and Outlook. An Artisan may seek rare materials, forgotten techniques, mastery, new customers, the chance to create something memorable, or a way to rebuild a livelihood disrupted by war or adventure. Playing an Artisan. Choose your craft and consider what workmanship catches your attention. The Background can shape how you view equipment and settlements, but it grants no Profession rank, Training Progress, reduced fee, faster training, or other mechanical Profession advantage. An Artisan may choose any Active Profession under the universal Profession rules exactly like any other character.

desc: Asmodae forms the northern half of shattered Atreia and is the homeland of the Asmodians. text: Asmodae Asmodae forms the northern half of shattered Atreia and is the homeland of the Asmodians. Perpetual night and colder conditions shaped its civilization, but the realm contains functioning cities, frontiers, varied mountains, frozen country, damaged lands under reclamation, and places of deep cultural memory. Pandaemonium Pandaemonium is the monumental capital of Asmodae, a great center of government, military organization, scholarship, religion, trade, and culture beneath the northern darkness. It is a functioning city rather than a fortress pretending to be one, with institutions and households that reflect centuries of Asmodian reconstruction. Pernon occupies the southern portion of the same island and serves as the capital’s cultivated residential counterpart. The city embodies the Asmodian conviction that civilization can flourish in a world shaped by hardship. Archons and other Daevas may come to Pandaemonium for orders, research, hearings, ceremonies, trade, institutional disputes, or the consequences of victories won elsewhere. Restricted military and sacred spaces coexist with ordinary civic life, giving the GM room for intrigue without making every visit a crisis. The capital should display craftsmanship, warmth, discipline, and beauty adapted to perpetual night rather than treating darkness as corruption. Pandaemonium is where Asmodae turns endurance into culture, law, memory, and ambition. Pernon Pernon is the cultivated residential counterpart to Pandaemonium, occupying the southern portion of the same island rather than existing as a distant independent landmass. Homes, gardens, workshops, gathering places, and carefully maintained spaces show a quieter expression of Asmodian life. Its beauty is adapted to darkness, emphasizing shelter, craft, community, and the visual character of the northern realm. The region gives domestic life a place beside the monumental institutions of the capital. For Daevas, Pernon can make centuries of Asmodian history personal through households, neighbors, artisans, celebrations, and obligations that persist between campaigns. Adventures here may involve community concerns, social investigation, family ties, or consequences carried home from the front. It is also an important reminder that Asmodians do not exist only as soldiers in an endless war. Pernon shows what endurance is meant to preserve: a life worth returning to. Ishalgen Ishalgen is a rugged island frontier whose terrain and isolated communities foster a strong sense of independence. Uneven ground, wilderness, exposed routes, and local settlements make the region feel removed from the monumental scale of Pandaemonium. Its people are accustomed to solving practical problems with limited support and to respecting dangers beyond settled ground. The landscape reflects the northern world without reducing it to a frozen wasteland. Daevas in Ishalgen may be asked to protect communities, cross difficult terrain, investigate remote disturbances, or deal with threats that cannot wait for distant authorities. Local knowledge and self-reliance matter here, making cooperation with residents as important as raw power. The region is well suited to grounded adventures where a small settlement can matter as much as a fortress objective. Ishalgen expresses Asmodian resilience through independence rather than through grand military spectacle. Altgard Altgard is a settled military frontier where Asmodian communities, roads, defenses, and patrol routes exist in close relationship with contested territory. Unlike the capital, its identity is shaped by the expectation that danger may arrive from beyond the next defended line. Soldiers and civilians share the same landscape, creating a region where preparedness is part of ordinary life. Its settlements demonstrate that a frontier can be both inhabited and militarily important. Archons operating in Altgard can expect patrols, escorts, reconnaissance, local defense, and missions where information about movement is as important as defeating an enemy. Communities should feel practiced in frontier life rather than permanently helpless, while Daevas provide the extraordinary force needed when ordinary defenses are exceeded. The region naturally supports stories about responsibility and the cost of keeping routes open. Altgard makes Asmodae’s military experience visible at the scale of roads, settlements, and watchful borders. Morheim Morheim is a mountainous and highly varied region, with sharp changes in terrain that make travel and local conditions unpredictable. Its identity is one of adaptability and defiance: communities and travelers learn quickly that one part of the region cannot stand for the whole. The landscape carries scars from major conflicts, and portions of Morheim have been profoundly altered by supernatural cold. Even so, the region remains more than the disasters that have struck it. Daevas in Morheim may move between mountain routes, settlements, damaged territory, and areas where old conflicts continue to shape present danger. Exploration and military operations can demand flexibility because terrain, weather, and strategic conditions change across the region. Stories here can focus on communities refusing to abandon difficult ground, as well as on the recovery of routes and places transformed by war. Morheim rewards characters who can adapt rather than assume every problem has the same solution. Beluslan Beluslan is the most strongly snowbound and frozen of Asmodae’s major regions, defined by severe cold, ice, and landscapes where survival infrastructure matters. Its settlements and routes exist because generations learned how to live with the environment rather than waiting for it to become gentle. The region carries a strong reclamation identity, with inhabited places standing beside damaged, dangerous, or difficult territory. Snow and darkness are part of home here, not symbols of evil. For Daevas, Beluslan can turn weather, distance, damaged routes, and isolated communities into meaningful parts of an adventure. Missions may involve reclaiming lost ground, protecting travelers, restoring access, investigating ruins, or confronting forces that exploit the region’s difficult conditions. Residents value competence and preparation, but that does not mean they are without warmth, art, or community. Beluslan shows Asmodian perseverance in one of its clearest physical forms. Brusthonin Brusthonin is a damaged but still living region shaped by contamination, loss, and long efforts at recovery. Parts of the land carry the consequences of Beritra-linked devastation, yet the region should never be presented as uniformly dead or beyond hope. Settlements, reclaimed ground, and people committed to restoration exist beside places that remain hazardous. Its defining cultural theme is patient recovery rather than simple ruin. Daevas who serve in Brusthonin may protect reclamation efforts, investigate contaminated sites, recover

title: Assassin
desc: Complete player reference for the Assassin class in Wings of Atreia, based on Player Handbook v3.10.
text: Melee Striker • Sneak Attack • Rune Marks • Execution Assassin “You'll know I'm there when you're dead.” Website rules source: Wings of Atreia Player Handbook v3.10 — Publication Master, 8 September 2026. This page preserves the handbook's class material and ordering. Class Identity Class Chassis Core Engine — Sneak Attack and Rune Marks Resource Flow — Generation, Recovery, Spending & Reset Specializations Preview Level 1–20 Action & Resource Reference Level-by-Level Progression Example Combat Sequences Specialization Reassignment The Assassin is a precision melee striker that builds target-bound Rune Marks, converts them into burst damage or execution riders, and uses Shadow Step to remain difficult to pin down. Unlike a conventional Extra Attack martial, its Level 5 Assassination Sequence is a conditional follow-up attack tied to a successful Sneak Attack. Class Identity Assassins are precision predators who win through positioning, timing, concealment, and carefully prepared execution. Their art is not simply “attacking from stealth.” An Assassin studies a target, creates the right opening, carves Rune Marks, and converts preparation into a sudden lethal advantage. Their greatest strength is the ability to decide where and when a close-range confrontation becomes dangerous. Tradition & Outlook The Assassin tradition descends from Atreia’s scout disciplines and is practiced by infiltrators, covert operatives, hunters of dangerous individuals, intelligence agents, and Daevas who favor certainty over spectacle. Assassins often prize patience, awareness, self-control, and economy of motion. Their motives vary widely: service to a faction, revenge, professional duty, protection through preemptive action, or the pursuit of perfect technique. Appearance & Adventuring Assassins favor equipment that permits mobility and unobstructed movement, with Shortswords and Daggers forming the class’s approved weapon identity in Wings of Atreia. Their appearance may be subdued or ceremonial, but practical Assassins avoid anything that compromises movement or control. They adventure when a threat must be found before it strikes, a route must be infiltrated, an enemy leader must be neutralized, or a mystery demands someone comfortable operating unseen. Website rules source: Wings of Atreia Player Handbook v3.10 — Publication Master, 8 September 2026. This page preserves the handbook's player-facing rules and terminology. Turn Structure & Actions Genuine Combat Initiative Round and Turn Action Economy Attack Action Universal Actions Ready Turn Structure & Actions Genuine Combat Initiative, rounds, and combat-only resources are used only for genuine combat or another situation where structured turn order is necessary. Characters cannot manufacture artificial combat to farm cooldowns, resources, or timing triggers. Initiative Initiative = 1d20 + Dexterity modifier. Do not add PB unless an explicit feature says so. Alert adds +2 Initiative. There is no Surprise Round and Surprise does not grant Advantage on Initiative. When one side genuinely catches another side unaware, the GM may, at discretion, allow one appropriate pre-Initiative attack roll against the target's normal defense before Initiative is rolled. This is not an extra round, is not automatic, and does not create a general Surprise action economy. After that resolution, roll Initiative normally. Round and Turn One combat round represents approximately six seconds in the game world. Each participant normally takes one turn in Initiative order. All turns in the round abstract actions occurring within the same six-second span; do not add each turn as another six seconds. Action Economy Action. One per turn. Movement. Up to the creature’s available movement, subject to terrain and conditions. Bonus Action. Up to one, but only when a feature grants something that uses a Bonus Action. Reaction. Normally one per round, refreshing at the start of the creature’s turn unless an explicit class rule says otherwise. Object interaction. One free simple object interaction per turn. There is no universal Action-to-Bonus-Action or Bonus-Action-to-Action conversion. Unused movement or Actions are not stored for later turns. Attack Action The Attack Action makes one attack unless a feature such as Extra Attack says otherwise. Grapple and Shove are full Actions and do not replace one attack within Extra Attack. Player Weapon Requirement. A player character must be wielding an approved class weapon to take the normal Attack Action. Unarmed Attacks and Improvised Weapons are not player combat options unless a later explicit feature creates a specific exception. Opportunity Attacks. Opportunity Attacks remain part of the core combat rules. When a hostile creature you can perceive voluntarily leaves your melee reach, you may use your Reaction to make one melee attack against it, resolving the attack before it leaves that reach. Forced movement does not provoke Opportunity Attacks unless an explicit rule says otherwise. Universal Actions Dash. Gain additional movement equal to your current Speed for the turn. Difficult Terrain and other movement costs still apply. While flying, Dash adds horizontal movement but does not grant an additional altitude-layer change. Disengage. Until the end of your turn, your movement does not provoke Opportunity Attacks. Dodge. Until the start of your next turn, attacks against you have Disadvantage if you can perceive the attacker, and you have Advantage on Dexterity saving throws. Dodge ends if you become Incapacitated or your Speed becomes 0. Hide. You must have meaningful concealment or another circumstance that allows hiding. Make Dexterity (Stealth) against Passive Perception or active Perception as appropriate. You cannot Hide while clearly seen. Hidden is not Invisible. Making an attack reveals your position after that attack resolves. Search. Deliberately search using a GM-selected check, commonly Wisdom (Perception) or Intelligence (Investigation). Use Object. Use this Action for substantial manipulation beyond the one free simple object interaction. A specific item’s activation rule controls when it states another cost. Ready A creature can prepare one Action for a perceivable trigger. When the trigger occurs, the creature may use its Reaction to perform the readied Action. Ready does not store ordinary movement, but Dash can be readied as the Action. Readied attacks retain all weapon properties. A readied spell must still meet implement and targeting requirements when released. Losing a mandatory implement before release prevents release. Concentration begins when the spell actually resolves. Ready never bypasses aerial restrictions, range, or other universal rules. Simultaneous Effects Effects resolve one at a time. The active creature orders its own simultaneous effects; the GM orders GM-controlled simultaneous effects. For opposing same-time effects, resolve the active creature first, then use Initiative if needed. Damage resolves before state changes caused by that damage. Start-of-turn and end-of-turn timing is literal. Reactions follow their trigger wording and are not inserted retroactively after the consequence has already resolved unless a rule explicitly allows it. Movement, Positioning & Physical Interaction Ground Movement Base Walk. 30 feet for a Daeva unless modified. Difficult Terrain. Costs 2 feet of movement for every 1 foot traveled. Prone. Standing from Prone requires one full Action and does not consume movement. A creature can move normally afterward if movement remains available. No universal Flanking. Opposite sides do not automatically grant Advantage. No universal Facing. Being behind a creature does not automatically grant Advantage. Occupied Spaces. A creature may move through a willing allied creature's space, treating that space as difficult terrain unless an explicit feature says otherwise. A creature cannot move through an enemy or neutral creature's occupied space unless an explicit rule permits it, and cannot end movement in another creature's occupied space unless an explicit rule allows it. Grapple and Shove Grapple and Shove each require a full Action. The target must be within reach and no more than one Size larger than you. Make Strength (Athletics) contested by the target’s choice of Strength (Athletics) or Dexterity (Acrobatics). On a successful Grapple, the target becomes Grappled; it may use its Action to escape by repeating the contest. Moving a Grappled creature costs 2 feet of movement for every 1 foot moved unless the target is at least two Sizes smaller than you. On a successful Shove, choose to push the target 5 feet or knock it Prone. Grapple and Shove do not replace attacks within the Attack Action and cannot substitute for Extra Attack. Player Weapon Requirement. Player characters do not use a universal Unarmed Attack damage rule; the normal Attack Action requires an approved class weapon unless an explicit feature says otherwise. Disarm Disarm is a full Action. The attacker uses Strength (Athletics) or Dexterity (Sleight of Hand), contested

It does not automatically grant Advantage, Expertise, a numerical bonus, or guaranteed success. Understanding Your Background Your Class describes what your character has learned to do as an adventuring Daeva. Your Background describes the life, training, profession, upbringing, or experiences that helped shape who they were before the campaign began. Faction tells you where you belong, Background helps explain where you came from, and Class describes how you operate as an adventurer. A Background does not determine your morality, personality, beliefs, faction loyalty, or future choices. Two characters with the same Background may have completely different lives and goals. Mechanically, use the Background table above exactly as written: choose two skills from your Background’s listed skill pool. The entries below add roleplaying context and do not grant additional rules benefits. Soldier What Is a Soldier?. A Soldier has meaningful experience with organized military service: troops, guards, scouts, officers, fortress personnel, or other disciplined fighting forces. Life and Origins. Military life may have included patrols, garrison duty, campaigns, escort work, reconnaissance, fortification defense, or service under a commander. That service may have occurred before or after ascension. Motivations and Outlook. Duty, loyalty, comradeship, ambition, patriotism, protection, regret, or the memory of fallen companions may still shape the character. A Soldier may respect military order, resent it, or be deciding what is truly worth fighting for. Playing a Soldier. Decide what kind of service shaped you, who you served beside, and what relationship you now have with authority and your former comrades. Being a Soldier does not require obedience or a martial Class. Scholar What Is a Scholar?. A Scholar has devoted part of their life to seeking, preserving, interpreting, or teaching knowledge. Scholars include researchers, historians, scribes, teachers, philosophers, archivists, investigators, and field specialists. Life and Origins. Study may have taken place under a teacher, within an archive or institution, or independently. Subjects can include history, geography, creatures, Aether, ruins, cultures, warfare, or any other serious field of inquiry. Motivations and Outlook. A Scholar may adventure to recover lost knowledge, investigate mysteries, study ruins or creatures directly, protect important discoveries, or prevent dangerous knowledge from being misused. Playing a Scholar. Choose the subject that fascinates you and decide whether you are an academic, a practical field researcher, or something between. Being scholarly does not require being socially awkward or confined to books. Acolyte What Is an Acolyte?. An Acolyte has meaningful experience with religious or spiritual service, sacred traditions, temples, ceremonies, or communities of worship. Life and Origins. The character may have been raised around a temple, studied under a religious teacher, volunteered in a sacred institution, maintained holy places, assisted ceremonies, or found faith after a life-changing event. Motivations and Outlook. Faith, service, protection, reform, doubt, duty, spiritual curiosity, or concern for a community may lead an Acolyte into adventure. An Acolyte can be devout, questioning, disillusioned, or seeking a new understanding. Playing an Acolyte. Decide what teachings shaped you and what relationship you have with them now. The Background does not require the Cleric or Chanter Class and does not automatically grant divine magic. Noble What Is a Noble?. A Noble was raised within a household or social circle possessing wealth, prestige, distinguished ancestry, political connections, or significant influence. Life and Origins. Noble life can involve etiquette, education, reputation, family expectations, household duties, rivalries, political arrangements, and the pressure of representing more than oneself. Motivations and Outlook. A Noble may seek to serve a family, escape its expectations, restore a reputation, establish an independent legacy, protect a household, or prove that personal worth is greater than inherited status. Playing a Noble. Decide whether you embrace, reject, exploit, or feel uncomfortable with your upbringing. Noble origin describes where you came from, not how you must behave. Outlander What Is an Outlander?. An Outlander has spent much of life beyond major population centers, among frontier settlements, wilderness regions, isolated communities, or people who travel far from established roads. Life and Origins. Hunters, trackers, guides, scouts, wanderers, remote settlers, and similar people learn to treat terrain, weather, wildlife, supplies, and isolation as ordinary concerns. Motivations and Outlook. An Outlander may adventure from wanderlust, duty to a remote home, curiosity about the wider world, a search for someone or something, or a desire to protect places others overlook. Playing an Outlander. Consider where you feel most at home and how you react to crowded cities or unfamiliar institutions. An Outlander need not be antisocial; the Background describes experience, not personality. Underworld What Is the Underworld?. Here, Underworld means the hidden networks of crime, illicit commerce, secrecy, unofficial influence, and socially marginal activity beneath respectable society. It does not mean a supernatural realm of the dead. Life and Origins. The character may have lived or worked among thieves, smugglers, fences, informants, lookouts, infiltrators, fixers, or others who survive through clandestine networks. They may also have entered such circles while working against them. Motivations and Outlook. Money, survival, freedom from former associates, revenge, protection, redemption, influence, or unfinished debts may draw the character onward. Playing an Underworld Character. Decide whether you left that life, remain connected to it, or were never truly a criminal at all. This Background does not require evil behavior or continuing criminal activity. Artisan What Is an Artisan?. An Artisan is a skilled maker whose life has been shaped by a practical craft. Smiths, armorers, carpenters, tailors, jewelers, cooks, builders, leatherworkers, and many other trades can fit this Background. Life and Origins. Training may come from family, a m

text: Balaurea Balaurea lies across the outer faces of shattered Atreia. Daevas know only a limited frontier in detail; beyond Inggison, Gelkmaros, and Silentera, Greater Balaurea remains vast, dangerous, and deliberately not exhaustively mapped. Inggison Inggison is the principal Elyos foothold on the known Balaurean frontier, reached through stable physical routes that can support real military logistics. It combines dangerous wilderness, ancient Balaur infrastructure, fortress corridors, expeditionary positions, and contact with peoples who have lived under Balaur pressure far longer than most Elyos newcomers. The region is a foothold, not a conquered province, and maintained routes become less certain as expeditions move beyond established corridors. Its approaches also form one side of the strategic access toward Silentera. Daevas in Inggison may defend fortresses, escort expeditions, work with Reians and other local peoples, explore ruins, or respond to Balaur activity in territory no faction fully controls. Success often depends on coalition-building and learning from residents rather than assuming Elyos institutions already understand the outer world. The frontier can support military missions and cultural encounters in the same journey. Inggison marks the point where the familiar war of Elysea opens into the much larger uncertainty of Balaurea. Gelkmaros Gelkmaros is the principal Asmodian foothold on the known Balaurean frontier, a dangerous outer-world region of wilderness, Balaur infrastructure, refugee communities, fortress corridors, and routes toward Silentera. Gelkmaros Fortress anchors Asmodian operations, while places such as Rhonnam Refugee Village, Vorgaltem Citadel, Crimson Temple, and other outposts reveal a frontier shared with communities that are not simply extensions of Asmodae. Old Balaur routes and structures remain embedded in the landscape. Control is practical and local rather than absolute. Archons and other Daevas may defend refugees, negotiate with local peoples, secure routes, investigate hostile infrastructure, or undertake expeditions beyond reliable maps. The region rewards field competence and the ability to protect without assuming that protection grants ownership or assimilation. Not every Shulack or other Balaurean people encountered here is automatically hostile, making judgment as important as combat readiness. Gelkmaros is where Asmodian resilience meets a world whose conflicts are older and more complicated than the familiar rivalry with Elysea. Silentera Canyon Silentera Canyon is a vast physical subterranean network of canyons, tunnels, chambers, ruins, and hidden routes linking the Inggison and Gelkmaros frontiers. It is neither a Rift network nor a separate dimension; Daevas enter an actual deep fracture system beneath the Balaurean frontier. No single modern faction controls the whole network, and knowledge of one mapped corridor does not imply knowledge of every branch. Beshmundir Temple is the greatest known deep site associated with these routes. For expeditionary Daevas, Silentera is a place of uncertain maps, ambushes, sealed ruins, difficult escape routes, and encounters where Elyos and Asmodian interests may collide far from reinforcement. Guides may know particular passages without understanding the entire system, while deeper areas remain contested, Balaur-dominated, or simply unexplored. The canyon supports dungeon exploration, rescue, espionage, archaeology, and situations where temporary cooperation can become more useful than faction pride. Every descent should reinforce the feeling that the known frontier is only a narrow opening into a much larger outer world. Greater Balaurea Beyond the known frontier lies an enormous outer world of wilderness, ruins, cities, Dragon Lord dominions, independent peoples, Drana zones, and infrastructure that Daevas have not exhaustively mapped. WoA intentionally leaves this greater territory open rather than importing every later location or storyline into the starting setting. Travel beyond maintained corridors should feel like genuine expedition into uncertain territory. Future campaigns may discover new settlements, routes, allies, enemies, and regions consistent with established WoA canon, but those discoveries are not predetermined. The known Balaurea frontier is therefore a beginning, not a complete atlas.

text: Bastion Targeting and Chassis The pilot and Bastion have separate HP and temporary HP. Repairs restore Bastion HP and are not healing. While occupied, ordinary physical attacks targeting the Aethertech generally strike the Bastion first. Mental, emotional, biological, and similar effects target the pilot when appropriate. One area effect normally does not double-hit both pilot and Bastion. Bastion physical STR/DEX/CON saves use PB + INT modifier. Mental saves use the pilot’s relevant save. When the Bastion reaches 0 HP it is Disabled. The pilot is ejected to the nearest legal space, takes 1d6 Force damage, and does not provoke Opportunity Attacks from the ejection. A disabled Bastion retains its current Core and Heat; a fresh chassis does not replace it. A Short Rest repairs a Disabled or damaged Bastion to half its maximum HP, if it currently has less HP than that amount. A Long Rest repairs the Bastion to its maximum HP. These restorations are repairs, not healing. Once the Bastion has at least 1 HP, it is operational. Entering or re-entering a deployed Bastion uses an Action when otherwise legal. A defeated or voluntarily replaced Bastion never functions as a companion or second PC. text: Beluslan Beluslan is the most strongly snowbound and frozen of Asmodae’s major regions, defined by severe cold, ice, and landscapes where survival infrastructure matters. Its settlements and routes exist because generations learned how to live with the environment rather than waiting for it to become gentle. The region carries a strong reclamation identity, with inhabited places standing beside damaged, dangerous, or difficult territory. Snow and darkness are part of home here, not symbols of evil. For Daevas, Beluslan can turn weather, distance, damaged routes, and isolated communities into meaningful parts of an adventure. Missions may involve reclaiming lost ground, protecting travelers, restoring access, investigating ruins, or confronting forces that exploit the region’s difficult conditions. Residents value competence and preparation, but that does not mean they are without warmth, art, or community. Beluslan shows Asmodian perseverance in one of its clearest physical forms.

text: Brusthonin Brusthonin is a damaged but still living region shaped by contamination, loss, and long efforts at recovery. Parts of the land carry the consequences of Beritra-linked devastation, yet the region should never be presented as uniformly dead or beyond hope. Settlements, reclaimed ground, and people committed to restoration exist beside places that remain hazardous. Its defining cultural theme is patient recovery rather than simple ruin. Daevas who serve in Brusthonin may protect reclamation efforts, investigate contaminated sites, recover lost history, escort workers, or confront threats that return to weakened ground. Progress can be slow and uneven, which makes small successes meaningful instead of insignificant. The people living here are participants in recovery, not scenery waiting to be rescued. Brusthonin allows campaigns to show that defending Atreia can mean healing a place as much as winning a battle.

text: Chain Attacks A Chain begins when you declare a successful melee hit on your own turn to be an Opener . You can maintain only one Chain at a time. The Chain belongs to you, not to a particular enemy, so later Links may strike another legal target. A miss does not automatically end the Chain. It lasts until the end of your next turn, until you use a Finisher, abandon it, or become unable to continue it. One Chain technique may modify a given attack. Chain Links and Finishers normally apply only to attacks made on your own turn. A Finisher ends the Chain after it resolves. Chain Dice are d6 at Levels 1–4, d8 at 5–10, d10 at 11–16, and d12 at 17–20. Chain Dice added directly to the triggering weapon attack double on a critical hit. Independent secondary damage does not.

title: Chanter
desc: Complete player reference for the Chanter class in Wings of Atreia, based on Player Handbook v3.10.
text: Martial Support • Mantras • Cadence • Harmonic Warfare Chanter “Stay close, stay safe.” Website rules source: Wings of Atreia Player Handbook v3.10 — Publication Master, 8 September 2026. This page preserves the handbook's class material and ordering. Spellcasting Reference: Chanter has a dedicated spell-list page for quick browsing. View Chanter Spell List → Class Identity Class Chassis Core Engine — Cadence Resource Flow — Generation, Recovery, Spending & Reset Spell List Specializations Preview Level 1–20 Action & Resource Reference Level-by-Level Progression Example Rhythm Sequence Specialization Reassignment The Chanter wins by alternating weapon attacks, spells, and active Mantra management. Cadence is earned by changing categories rather than repeating one action, then spent on damage, protection, healing, and tactical movement. It is a secondary healer and hybrid support, not a replacement for the Cleric or a dedicated martial striker. Class Identity Chanters are martial support specialists who combine staff technique, enchantment, restorative magic, and Mantras into a continuous rhythm of battle. Rather than solving every problem through one large spell, a Chanter improves the party’s performance over time and responds to changing pressure with Cadence. Their presence is felt in how effectively the entire group moves, strikes, and recovers together. Tradition & Outlook The Chanter tradition grows from Atreia’s priestly disciplines but emphasizes disciplined body, voice, repetition, and the shaping of Aether through words and practiced forms. Chanters are often teachers, battle companions, spiritual guides, martial ascetics, or morale-keepers. They tend to value harmony between individual excellence and collective strength: the ideal Chanter does not merely stand beside allies but helps those allies become more capable. Appearance & Adventuring Chanters are strongly associated with Staff and Quarterstaff techniques in Wings of Atreia. Their clothing and armor tend to allow movement while retaining the ceremonial or disciplined character of a priestly warrior. They adventure to guide companions, strengthen military or exploratory groups, carry teachings into dangerous places, preserve morale during long campaigns, or prove that disciplined cooperation can overcome enemies stronger than any one Daeva. Class Chassis Trait Rule Primary Ability Intelligence Secondary Ability Charisma Hit Die d8 Saving Throws Constitution, Intelligence Armor Chain Armor Weapons Staff, Quarterstaff Skills Choose 2: Arcana, History, Insight, Medicine, Performance, Persuasion, Religion Spellcasting Ability INT Mantra Ability CHA Signature Resource Cadence Spell Advancements +1 each level after 1; 19 total Maximum Spell Level 7 Extra Attack Level 5; two attacks only Core Engine — Cadence Cadence is a genuine-combat resource. It begins at 0 when combat starts, resets to 0 when combat ends, and artificial initiative cannot create or restore it. Maximum Cadence is 3 at Levels 1–4, 4 at 5–8, 5 at 9–12, 6 at 13–16, and 7 at 17–20. Category Qualifying Event Martial You hit a hostile creature with a weapon attack. Spell A Chanter spell meaningfully affects a creature by hit, damage, failed save, actual healing, meaningful prevention, or another significant effect. Chant You activate, replace, or deliberately invoke a Mantra/Chant and it meaningfully changes at least one creature. Passive maintenance never qualifies. Your previous qualifying category is always the most recent successful qualifying category, whether or not that event generated Cadence. When you successfully complete a qualifying event whose category differs from your previous successful qualifying category, gain 1 Cadence, subject to the normal generation limit. Your first successful qualifying event in a combat establishes your previous category; it does not generate Cadence by itself. Normal Cadence generation is limited to 1 per turn unless a feature explicitly grants more. Secondary Chanter riders do not recursively generate Cadence, Resonant Network triggers, Mantra Weaving, or other support sequences unless explicit. Resource Flow — Generation, Recovery, Spending & Reset Resource Flow Rule Starting State Cadence begins at 0 when genuine combat starts and resets to 0 when combat ends. Maximum 3 at Levels 1–4; 4 at 5–8; 5 at 9–12; 6 at 13–16; 7 at 17–20. Qualifying Categories Martial: a weapon attack hits a hostile. Spell: a Chanter spell meaningfully affects a creature. Chant: you activate, replace, or deliberately invoke a Mantra/Chant and it meaningfully changes at least one creature; passive maintenance does not qualify. How You Gain It When a successful qualifying event uses a category different from your previous successful qualifying category, gain 1 Cadence. The first successful qualifying event of a combat only establishes the previous category. Generation Limits Normal generation is capped at 1 Cadence per turn unless an explicit feature increases it. The previous category updates after every successful qualifying event whether or not Cadence was generated. How You Spend It Resonant Strike 1 Cadence; Guarding Rhythm 1 Cadence; Restorative Verse 2 Cadence. Other Chanter features spend Cadence only when their text states a cost. Refunds / Overflow Later features may refund Cadence, create Rhythm Steps, or convert excess Cadence into other benefits. Those are explicit class effects, not new base generation. Reset / Anti-Farming Cadence resets to 0 when combat ends. Artificial Initiative, passive Mantra maintenance, and secondary riders do not create or restore it unless explicit. Choose Elyos or Asmodian. 2. Choose one of the 11 classes. 3. Assign 16, 14, 14, 12, 10, 8 among STR, DEX, CON, INT, WIS and CHA. 4. Choose one Background. 5. Universal Daeva Traits Trait Rule Creature Type Humanoid (Daeva) Size Medium Walking Speed 30 ft Darkvision 60 ft Ageless Living beings who do not age normally. Manifest Wings Every Daeva has functional Common Wings. Aether-Dependent Flight Flight depends on local Aether conditions. Aetheric Reconstitution A Daeva who truly dies may reform through a functioning attuned Obelisk under the reconstitution rules. Starting Equipment & Kinah Every character begins with one fixed base class weapon or implement, one armor set, Common Wings, and starting Kinah. No character automatically receives potions, ammunition bundles, upgraded equipment, extra adventuring gear, or a shield unless a class feature or other explicit rule grants it. Starting Kinah = 500 Kinah + 250 Kinah for each character level above 1. A Level 1 character starts with 500 Kinah; a Level 20 character starts with 5,250 Kinah. Abilities and the 18 Skills A skill is a trained way of applying an ability. The GM chooses the ability that best fits the approach; the familiar ability below is the normal pairing. These are player-use explanations, not new automatic bonuses. Skill Usual Ability What It Lets You Attempt Acrobatics DEX Balance, controlled movement, tumbling, landing and physically awkward agility. Animal Handling WIS Calm, understand, direct or manage ordinary trainable creatures. Arcana INT Magic, Aether theory, magical phenomena, spell structures and intellectual Aether analysis. Athletics STR Climb, jump, swim, grapple-related exertion and other raw physical effort. Deception CHA Mislead, bluff, conceal intent, maintain a false story or impersonate. History INT Recall public history, cultures, institutions, conflicts and notable people or places. Insight WIS Read motives, sincerity, emotional state and social intent; not mind reading. Intimidation CHA Pressure, threaten or project authority when coercion is plausible. Investigation INT Reason from clues, search methodically, understand mechanisms and reconstruct events. Medicine WIS Stabilize a dying creature, diagnose injuries/afflictions and administer relevant care. Nature INT Terrain, plants, ordinary wildlife, ecosystems, weather and natural hazards. Perception WIS Notice creatures, ambushes, sounds, traps, hidden details and immediate sensory changes. Performance CHA Sing, act, dance, entertain or sustain a deliberate artistic performance. Persuasion CHA Negotiate, appeal, request cooperation or change a position when plausible. Religion INT Doctrines, rites, religious history, sacred customs and spiritual traditions. Sleight of Hand DEX Precise manual manipulation, theft, mechanisms and physical Aether interaction when called for. Stealth DEX Hide, move quietly, remain unnoticed or maintain concealment. Survival WIS Track, navigate, read wilderness signs, avoid becoming lost and manage wilderness operations. Proficiency vs. Expertise. Proficiency adds PB once. Expertise doubles the PB contribution for one proficient Skill. A duplicate proficiency never becomes Expertise automatically. It does not automatically grant Advantage, Expertise, a numerical bonus, or guaranteed success. Understanding Your Background Your Class describes what your character has learned to do as an adventuring Daeva. Your Background describes the life, training, profession, upbringing, or experiences that helped shape who they were before the campaign began. Faction tells you where you belong, Background helps explain where you came from, and Class describes how you operate as an adventurer. A Background does not determine your morality, personality, beliefs, faction loyalty, or future choices. Two characters with the same Background may have completely different lives and goals. title: Character Creation & Advancement
desc: Do I choose a race or species? No. Every standard player character is a Daeva . Choose Elyos or Asmodian as faction/culture. The two factions use the same universal Daeva mechanical foundation. How do I assign Ability Scores? Assign 16, 14, 14, 12, 10, and 8 freely among STR, DEX, CON, INT, WIS, and CHA. There is no ability-score rolling or point buy. Can I
text: Character Creation & Advancement Do I choose a race or species? No. Every standard player character is a Daeva . Choose Elyos or Asmodian as faction/culture. The two factions use the same universal Daeva mechanical foundation. How do I assign Ability Scores? Assign 16, 14, 14, 12, 10, and 8 freely among STR, DEX, CON, INT, WIS, and CHA. There is no ability-score rolling or point buy. Can I multiclass? No. A Daeva advances in one class from Level 1 through Level 20. Do characters gain XP? No. Advancement is Milestone only . The GM awards levels for meaningful campaign progress. When do I choose an ASI or Feat? Universal ASI/Feat choices occur at Levels 4, 8, 12, and 16 . Level 19 grants an Empyrean Boon , not another normal ASI/Feat choice. What does a Background give me? A Background gives exactly two Skill Proficiencies chosen from that Background's eligible skill list and can establish narrative relevance or permission where appropriate. It does not automatically grant Advantage, Expertise, or guaranteed success. Does duplicate proficiency become Expertise? No. Proficiency adds PB once. Expertise exists only when an explicit feature grants it. Can I change my Specialization after choosing it? Yes, but only at the normal reassignment checkpoints. Choose your initial Specialization at Level 3 . When gaining Level 6, Level 10, and Level 14 , you may either continue your current Specialization or switch to another Specialization available to your class. The Level 14 decision is the final normal Specialization choice through Level 20. If I switch Specializations, do I keep features from my old path? No. Remove every feature granted by the previous Specialization and replace it with the new Specialization's complete feature package through the current checkpoint. Features from different paths cannot be mixed or retained. Make any choices required by newly gained features, and remove, reselect, or recalculate path-dependent options, capacities, and maxima as necessary. Reassignment itself restores no HP or class resources, and current values cannot remain above a new maximum. Can I change Specialization during downtime or by training? No. Normal reassignment happens only while gaining Level 6, 10, or 14. Rest, downtime, training, ordinary retraining, or time between adventures does not create an extra reassignment opportunity.

Vision, Stealth, Traps, Locks & Theft Vision and Light Cover, Line of
text: Chases, Morale, Escorts & Creature Transport Player Rules Exploration & Interaction Vision, stealth, traps, locks, theft, hazards, social rules, chases, and loot. Website rules source: Wings of Atreia Player Handbook v3.10 — Publication Master, 8 September 2026. This page preserves the handbook's player-facing rules and terminology. Vision, Stealth, Traps, Locks & Theft Vision and Light Cover, Line of Sight & Line of Effect Stealth and Infiltration Traps and Non-Aether Hazards Locks Theft and Pickpocket Social Interaction, Information & Captivity Vision, Stealth, Traps, Locks & Theft Vision and Light Light states are Bright Light, Dim Light, and Darkness. Obscuration states are Lightly Obscured and Heavily Obscured. Dim Light lightly obscures; Darkness heavily obscures a creature that cannot otherwise see through it. Daeva Darkvision treats Darkness within 60 feet as Dim Light, not Bright Light. A recommended ordinary light source has a stated Bright radius plus an equal additional Dim radius unless its own text says otherwise. Bright light does not universally prohibit Stealth. Obscurity and Invisibility do not automatically make a creature Hidden. Cover, Line of Sight & Line of Effect No Cover. No defensive benefit from Cover. Half Cover. A creature or object behind meaningful partial obstruction gains +2 AC and +2 to Dexterity saving throws against effects originating from the covered direction. Intervening creatures can provide Half Cover when they materially obstruct the line. Full Cover. Full Cover blocks the relevant Line of Effect and prevents direct targeting through that obstruction unless an explicit rule says otherwise. Three-Quarters Cover does not exist in Wings of Atreia. Cover does not stack; use the best applicable Cover. Altitude neither inherently grants nor ignores Cover. Line of Sight and Line of Effect are distinct. Line of Sight determines whether you can see a target or point. Line of Effect determines whether an attack, spell, or effect can physically reach it. Heavy obscurement is not Cover by itself. Stealth and Infiltration Use scene states Undetected, Suspicious, and Alerted; these are not Conditions. Stealth must exceed Passive Perception; ties favor the observer. An active Search uses the GM-selected check, commonly Wisdom (Perception) or Intelligence (Investigation), against the relevant DC or opposing Stealth; ties favor the Searcher where opposed. Do not reroll Stealth every 5 feet; roll again only when circumstances materially change. For group Stealth, at least half the group must succeed. A failed check may create Suspicion rather than immediate full alarm when appropriate. Distractions create an opportunity to Hide rather than automatic success. Disguises are primarily social. Invisibility is not the same as Hidden. Wings do not automatically prevent Stealth. Traps and Non-Aether Hazards Describe a hazard with Trigger, Detection, Avoid/Disable method, Save/Check, Effect, and Reset/Duration. Hazards may be obvious, concealed, or hidden. Detection normally uses Passive Perception, active Perception, or Investigation. Disable methods depend on the mechanism and can use Sleight of Hand, Investigation, Athletics, or another appropriate Skill. There is no mandatory Thieves’ Tools system. Failure triggers the hazard only when the hazard says so. Damage and Conditions use existing universal rules. Forced movement is horizontal unless the hazard explicitly creates vertical displacement. Hazards normally resolve when triggered rather than taking their own Initiative turns. Repeat attempts require changed circumstances. Locks Mechanical Lock DC Simple 10 Standard 12 Secure 15 High Security 18 Exceptional 20+ The correct key opens a normal lock without a check. Mechanical locks generally use Dexterity (Sleight of Hand). Unusual mechanisms can use Intelligence (Investigation). Forcing uses Strength (Athletics); destroying a lock or door uses normal object/destruction adjudication. Failure does not automatically break or trigger a lock unless its design says so. Aether locks use Aether Interaction. If a task is impossible, do not assign an absurd DC—state that it cannot be done by that method. Theft and Pickpocket A theft attempt requires a plausible opportunity. Taking an accessible small item uses Dexterity (Sleight of Hand) against Passive Perception and must exceed it. If the target is actively watching, oppose with active Perception; ties favor the observer. Secured items can require a different approach. Failure may create suspicion or alarm. Success means the theft was unnoticed at that moment; later discovery remains possible. Distraction creates opportunity rather than automatic success. Help can grant +2 when genuinely meaningful. Worn armor, shields, Wings, wielded weapons, and equipped mandatory implements cannot simply be pickpocketed. Repeated attempts require changed circumstances. Social Interaction, Information & Captivity Attitudes NPC attitudes are Friendly, Neutral, or Hostile. Roleplay comes first; a roll is used only when outcome and consequence are uncertain. Common skills include Persuasion, Deception, Intimidation, Insight, and Investigation. Plausibility A social check cannot force an impossible concession or make an NPC believe something fundamentally implausible without exceptional circumstances. Leverage affects what is possible and can influence DCs, but it does not automatically grant Advantage. Interrogation An interrogated NPC can reveal only information they actually know. Resolve one meaningful line of questioning at a time. Failure may close that approach, create resistance, or produce consequences; repeated checks need changed circumstances. Insight is not mind reading. Deception may oppose Insight when appropriate. Intimidation can succeed while still creating later consequences. Information Gathering Information comes from plausible sources. Common knowledge needs no roll. Use the skill that matches the approach. Rumors may be Reliable, Uncertain, or False, but the GM does not label them for the players. Independent sources and evidence can verify claims. Restricted information requires access. There is no fixed universal gathering-time formula and no check spam. Captivity and Restraints Physical restraints use Restrained when their actual effect warrants it. Binding an unwilling conscious creature in combat requires control first and normally an Action. Escape can use Sleight of Hand, Athletics, or Acrobatics against the restraint’s DC. A locked cell does not automatically impose Restrained. Restrained does not inherently prevent spellcasting, but implement and action requirements still matter. Ordinary restraints do not suppress Wings, Aetheric Reconstitution, or class powers unless an explicit specialized restraint says so. Transporting prisoners uses ordinary logistics. Interrogation remains a separate social procedure. Chases, Morale, Escorts & Creature Transport Chases Band Approximate Separation Eng

title: Cleric
desc: Complete player reference for the Cleric class in Wings of Atreia, based on Player Handbook v3.10.
text: Primary Healer • Divine Grace • Protection • Purification Cleric “Protect me and you shall never fall.” Website rules source: Wings of Atreia Player Handbook v3.10 — Publication Master, 8 September 2026. This page preserves the handbook's class material and ordering. Spellcasting Reference: Cleric has a dedicated spell-list page for quick browsing. View Cleric Spell List → Class Identity Class Chassis Resource Flow — Generation, Recovery, Spending & Reset Spell List Specializations Preview Level 1–20 Action & Resource Reference Level-by-Level Progression Example Support Sequence Tradition & Outlook Specialization Reassignment The Cleric is Wings of Atreia’s primary restorative spellcaster. It is deliberately more durable than the d6 full casters and is rewarded for meaningful intervention: healing an ally in real danger, actually preventing damage, or removing a significant hostile effect. Divine Grace then converts that successful support into more emergency power. Class Identity Clerics are Atreia’s foremost restorative and protective spellcasters. Their calling is not limited to healing wounds after the fact: they preserve the party through recovery, cleansing, protection, and timely intervention while retaining the ability to fight when necessary. Divine Grace represents the reserve of sacred and restorative power through which a Cleric answers moments of genuine need. Tradition & Outlook The Cleric tradition grows from Atreia’s priestly disciplines and is associated with healers, battlefield ministers, temple servants, protectors of communities, and Daevas who understand survival as a collective responsibility. Clerics often value service, perseverance, mercy, duty, or faith, but they need not share one personality or theology. A militant Cleric and a gentle healer may practice the same class through very different convictions. Appearance & Adventuring Clerics commonly combine durable armor with practical healing or ritual equipment. In Wings of Atreia they may use Maces, Hammers, Staffs, Quarterstaffs, and shields from Round Shields to Medium Shields according to their approved access. They adventure to protect lives, confront corruption or supernatural danger, recover sacred knowledge, serve a cause, or ensure that an expedition can survive places where retreat and ordinary medicine are not enough. Long Rest restores all; Short Rest restores PB. Once per round, when you Meaningfully Support yourself or an ally with a Cleric spell or feature, regain 1 Grace. Your normal once-per-round generation becomes available again at the start of your turn, allowing an off-turn protection to qualify without double-dipping around initiative boundaries. Meaningful Support means one of the following actually occurs: restore HP while the creature was below half maximum HP; prevent or reduce damage by at least PB; or suppress/remove a mechanically significant hostile condition or effect. Healing a full-HP creature, preventing 0 damage, refreshing temporary HP without increasing it, cosmetic effects, or intentionally manufactured harmless damage do not qualify. Self-support must satisfy the same standard. Temporary HP are not healing and cannot restore a creature from 0 HP. Passive aura bonuses and passive AC do not generate Divine Grace unless a feature explicitly says so. A secondary Cleric rider created by another Cleric feature does not recursively trigger Twin Devotion, Sacred Intervention, Graceful Channeling, Empowered Restoration, or another support sequence unless explicit. Only one Cleric rolled-healing class rider normally modifies the same individual healing instance, except Graceful Restoration may coexist with one specialization rolled-healing rider. Flat Cleric save penalties do not stack; use the largest. Resource Flow — Generation, Recovery, Spending & Reset Resource Flow Rule Starting State Divine Grace is a rest-based reserve. It does not automatically reset to 0 when combat starts or ends; later features can establish a minimum starting amount. Maximum PB + WIS modifier, minimum 2. Rest Recovery Long Rest restores all Divine Grace. Short Rest restores Grace equal to PB, up to maximum. How You Gain It Once per round, regain 1 Grace when a Cleric spell or feature Meaningfully Supports you or an ally: healing while the recipient was below half HP, preventing/reducing at least PB damage, or suppressing/removing a mechanically significant hostile condition or effect. Generation Timing Your normal once-per-round generation becomes available again at the start of your turn. This lets a qualifying off-turn protection generate Grace without double-dipping across initiative boundaries. Does Not Qualify Healing a full-HP creature, preventing 0 damage, refreshing temporary HP without increasing it, passive aura/AC alone, cosmetic effects, or manufactured harmless damage do not generate Grace. How You Spend It Graceful Restoration 1 Grace; Protective Grace 1 Grace; Cleansing Grace 1 Grace; Purifier Absolute Purification 1 Grace; Level 20 Divine Presence save reroll 1 Grace. Other Cleric features spend Grace only when their text states a cost. Grace Momentum can reduce the first eligible technique cost. Refunds / Secondary Effects Later refunds and support riders follow their own timing. A secondary Cleric rider does not recursively generate new support sequences unless explicitly stated.
