This page preserves the handbook's class material and ordering. Spellcasting Reference: Songweaver has a dedicated spell-list page for quick browsing. View Songweaver Spell List → Class Identity Class Chassis Resource Flow — Generation, Recovery, Spending & Reset Spell List Specializations Preview Level 1–20 Action & Resource Reference Level-by-Level Progression Example Performance Sequence Tradition & Outlook Specialization Reassignment The Songweaver changes battlefield purpose from moment to moment. Every Songweaver spell belongs to Harmony, Guard, Dissonance, or Requiem. Successful performances create short-lived Refrains, changing Song Roles builds Resonance, and Resonance is spent to amplify, sustain, counter, or conduct the performance. Class Identity Songweavers shape Aether through music, using performance as destructive spellcraft, support, control, and restoration. Their strength lies in versatility: the same class can pressure an enemy, sustain an ally, or shift the emotional and tactical rhythm of an encounter. Resonance represents the accumulating harmony between performance, spellcraft, and the unfolding battle. Tradition & Outlook The Songweaver tradition is rooted in Atreia’s Muses and in remembrance of Siel. The wider Aion tradition describes Muses who continued their studies after the Cataclysm and eventually joined music with Aether in service to their people; their battlefield contribution led to recognition as an established Daeva class. Songweavers may therefore approach performance as remembrance, artistry, scholarship, service, or a declaration that beauty still has power in a broken world. Appearance & Adventuring Songweavers use Lutes and Lyres as their approved implements, often making instrument, costume, gesture, and magical display part of a single visible identity. Their appearance can range from formal performer to traveling battle-musician without changing class mechanics. They adventure to preserve stories, honor Siel, inspire allies, master Aetheric music, carry culture into war-torn regions, or use beauty and sound as weapons against forces that would reduce Atreia to silence. Class Chassis Trait Rule Primary Ability Charisma Secondary Ability Intelligence Hit Die d6 Saving Throws Charisma, Dexterity Armor Cloth Focus Lute, Lyre, or suitable magical instrument Skills Choose 3: Arcana, Deception, Insight, Performance, Persuasion, History, Religion Spellcasting Ability CHA Technical Refrain Ability INT Signature Resource Resonance Spell Advancements +2 each level after 1; 38 total Maximum Spell Level 9 Extra Attack None Song Roles and Resonance Song Role Primary Function Harmony Healing and positive support Guard Protection and defensive enhancement Dissonance Debuffs and control Requiem Offensive magical pressure Track the most recent Song Role of a Songweaver spell that successfully affected at least one creature, whether or not that casting generated Resonance. Resonance is genuine-combat only: it begins at 0, resets to 0 at combat end, and artificial initiative cannot generate it. Maximum Resonance is 3 at Levels 1–4, 4 at 5–8, 5 at 9–12, 6 at 13–16, and 7 at 17–20. After a Songweaver spell resolves, if that casting satisfies at least one of the generation conditions below, gain 1 Resonance, subject to the normal per-turn limit. The first successful Song Role in a combat establishes role history for Contrasting Verse; it cannot contrast with a role that does not yet exist. Harmonic Support: a single Songweaver spell meaningfully benefits two or more creatures. Dissonant Performance: a single Songweaver spell meaningfully affects two or more hostile creatures. Contrasting Verse: you successfully cast a Songweaver spell whose Song Role differs from your previous successful Song Role. Each generation condition triggers at most once per casting. Normal generation is capped at 1 Resonance per turn unless a feature explicitly increases it. A Refrain, Chorus Echo, Resonance rider, specialization rider, or other secondary Songweaver effect cannot recursively generate Resonance, create/trigger another Refrain, or activate another Songweaver rider unless explicit. Resource Flow — Generation, Recovery, Spending & Reset Resource Flow Rule Starting State Resonance begins at 0 in genuine combat and resets to 0 when combat ends. Maximum 3 at Levels 1–4; 4 at 5–8; 5 at 9–12; 6 at 13–16; 7 at 17–20. How You Gain It After a Songweaver spell resolves, if the casting satisfies at least one generation condition, gain 1 Resonance, subject to the normal per-turn limit. Harmonic Support A single Songweaver spell meaningfully benefits two or more creatures. Dissonant Performance A single Songweaver spell meaningfully affects two or more hostile creatures. Contrasting Verse The successfully cast Songweaver spell uses a Song Role different from your previous successful Song Role. The first successful role in combat only establishes role history. Generation Limits Each condition triggers at most once per casting, and a casting still produces only the amount permitted by the current per-turn generation cap. Normal base generation is capped at 1 Resonance per turn unless a feature explicitly increases it. Spending / Reset Crescendo 1 Resonance; Sustaining Note 1; Countermelody 1; later Songweaver features state their own Resonance costs. Secondary Refrain/Chorus/rider effects do not recursively generate Resonance. Resonance resets to 0 when combat ends. text: Level-by-Level Progression Full Caster • Elemental Damage • Aether Focus • Spell Shaping Sorcerer “This will only hurt for a second.” Website rules source: Wings of Atreia Player Handbook v3.10 — Publication Master, 8 September 2026. This page preserves the handbook's class material and ordering. Spellcasting Reference: Sorcerer has a dedicated spell-list page for quick browsing. View Sorcerer Spell List → Class Identity Class Chassis Core Engine — Aether Focus Resource Flow — Generation, Recovery, Spending & Reset Spell List Specializations Preview Level 1–20 Action & Resource Reference Level-by-Level Progression Spellcasting Example Specialization Reassignment The Sorcerer is the raw magical-damage benchmark. It casts through Fire, Ice, Lightning, and Wind spell chains, then spends Aether Focus only when a particular spell needs more damage, area, control pressure, or reliability. Aether Focus enhances spells; it is never the fuel required to cast ordinary Sorcerer spells. Class Identity Sorcerers are masters of direct Aetheric spellcraft, combining destructive magic with the ability to control the shape and tempo of a fight. They can punish clustered enemies, deny movement or action, and unleash powerful spells when an opening appears. Aether Focus represents the concentration and arcane discipline required to turn immense magical potential into reliable battlefield power. Tradition & Outlook The Sorcerer tradition grows from Atreia’s mage disciplines and is associated with formal magical study, experimentation, academies, battlefield arcanists, and Daevas fascinated by the structure of Aether itself. Sorcerers commonly value knowledge, precision, preparation, and intellectual mastery, although their personalities range from scholarly restraint to spectacular confidence. For many, magic is both a weapon and a language through which Atreia can be understood. Appearance & Adventuring Sorcerers favor cloth armor and magical implements such as Orbs and Spellbooks under the Wings of Atreia equipment rules. Their appearance may reflect academic, military, ceremonial, or highly individual magical traditions. They adventure to recover lost knowledge, study Aetheric phenomena, test magical theories, defend their people with overwhelming spellcraft, or confront powers that ordinary weapons cannot adequately answer. Class Chassis Trait Rule Primary Ability Intelligence Secondary Ability Wisdom Hit Die d6 Saving Throws Constitution, Intelligence Armor Cloth Implements Magical Orbs, Spellbooks Spellcasting Ability INT Spell Save DC 8 + PB + INT modifier Spell Attack PB + INT modifier Signature Resource Aether Focus Spell Advancements +2 every class level after 1; 38 total Maximum Spell Level 9 Extra Attack None Core Engine — Aether Focus Maximum Aether Focus equals PB + INT modifier, minimum 2. A Long Rest restores all expended Aether Focus. A Short Rest restores Aether Focus equal to PB, up to your maximum. The resource is an enhancement reserve: casting an ordinary Sorcerer spell never requires Aether Focus unless a spell or class feature explicitly says otherwise. Resource Flow — Generation, Recovery, Spending & Reset Resource Flow Rule Starting State Aether Focus is a rest-based enhancement reserve and does not reset merely because combat begins or ends. After a Long Rest it is normally full. Maximum PB + INT modifier, minimum 2. Aether Sage and the Level 20 capstone can explicitly increase this maximum. Rest Recovery Long Rest restores all expended Aether Focus. Short Rest restores Focus equal to PB, up to maximum; Aether Sage can improve this recovery. Base Generation The base Sorcerer does not generate Aether Focus from ordinary spell hits or damage. Combat refunds exist only where a class or specialization feature explicitly grants them. How You Spend It Intensify 1 Focus; Widen 1 Focus; Potent Control 1 Focus; other Sorcerer features spend Aether Focus only when their text states a cost. Ordinary spellcasting costs no Focus. Refunds / Discounts Aether Sage and later features may discount a shaping cost or refund Focus after a qualifying shaped spell. A refund is not a second casting or a new spell trigger. Persistence Unused Aether Focus persists between encounters until spent or restored. Important Distinction Aether Focus is a Sorcerer class resource. It is not environmental Aether, Refined Aether, an Aether State, or a universal damage type. Your spirit is with you.” Website rules source: Wings of Atreia Player Handbook v3.10 — Publication Master, 8 September 2026. This page preserves the handbook's class material and ordering. Spellcasting Reference: Spiritmaster has a dedicated spell-list page for quick browsing. View Spiritmaster Spell List → Class Identity Class Chassis Core Engine — Summon Spirit Resource Flow — Generation, Recovery, Spending & Reset Spell List Specializations Preview Level 1–20 Action & Resource Reference Level-by-Level Progression Example Combat Sequence Specialization Reassignment The Spiritmaster is a two-body tactical caster. One active elemental spirit shares the Spiritmaster’s turn and action economy; together they equal one complete player character. The class establishes two battlefield positions, casts through the spirit, and earns Spirit Bond only through meaningful master-spirit coordination. Class Identity Spiritmasters are binders and commanders of elemental spirits who fight as a partnership rather than as a solitary caster. Their strength comes from coordinating their own spellcraft with a Greater Spirit, applying pressure, disruption, and control across more than one position on the battlefield. Spirit Bond represents the relationship and command structure that makes this divided presence function as one class. Tradition & Outlook The Spiritmaster tradition develops from Atreia’s mage disciplines but turns outward toward spirits, elemental forces, and the difficult art of directing entities shaped by Aether. Spiritmasters are often patient observers, researchers, summoners, or specialists in threats that cannot be understood through ordinary physical study. Their beliefs about spirits differ: some emphasize command, others partnership, responsibility, curiosity, or respect for elemental power. Appearance & Adventuring Spiritmasters use cloth armor and magical implements, while the visible presence of a summoned spirit often defines their silhouette more strongly than clothing does. Their equipment may include ritual, scholarly, or elemental motifs without creating additional mechanics. They adventure to understand unusual spirits, recover lost summoning knowledge, counter supernatural threats, serve as versatile magical operatives, or deepen the bond between Daeva and elemental ally. Only one Spiritmaster spirit may normally be active. Summoning uses an Action and places the spirit in a visible unoccupied space within 15 feet. A defeated spirit disperses into Aether, makes no death saves, and cannot be resummoned until the start of your next turn. Outside combat a newly summoned spirit appears at full HP; voluntary replacement during combat preserves the dismissed spirit’s current HP percentage rather than healing by switching forms. text: Level-by-Level Progression Level 1 — Resolve, Resolute Guard, Challenge, Guardian’s Intercession You gain the complete Resolve engine and the three signature defensive mechanics described above. Maximum Resolve is 3 and your Guard Die is d6. Level 2 — Combat Discipline and Protective Reflexes Shield Discipline: while wielding a shield, the first time each round an attack redirected through Guardian’s Intercession hits you, reduce its damage by PB before Resolute Guard. Weapon Discipline: once on each of your turns when you hit with a one-handed melee weapon, add PB to that attack’s damage. Fortress Discipline: while wearing Plate, forced movement against you is reduced by 5 ft, minimum 0, and you have Advantage on checks and saves to resist Prone. Vanguard Discipline: once each turn after moving at least 10 ft toward a hostile and ending within melee reach, you may move through hostile spaces during that movement; you cannot end occupied and OAs against you during it have Disadvantage. Retraining is available at class Feat/ASI levels. Protective Reflexes: after successful Guardian’s Intercession, the protected ally may move up to 5 ft without provoking from the creature whose attack you intercepted, if it can legally move. Level 3 — Templar Specialization Choose one Specialization and gain its Level 3 advancement. The full path preview appears above so you can see where each choice leads. Specialization Level 3 Advancement Bulwark Unyielding Intercession Justicar Retributive Challenge Aegis Hold the Ground Choose Bulwark, Justicar, or Aegis. Specialization milestones occur at Levels 3, 6, 10, and 14. Bulwark — Unyielding Intercession: Intercession range becomes 10 ft; when the ally is more than 5 ft away, you may move up to 5 ft toward it as part of the Reaction without provoking, but must end within 5 ft. Justicar — Retributive Challenge: when a Challenged creature triggers Defy the Templar, after its attack resolves you may use your Reaction to make one melee weapon attack against it if it is in reach. Aegis — Hold the Ground: while not Incapacitated, spaces within 5 ft of you are difficult terrain for hostile creatures; creatures you permit are unaffected. Level 4 — Feat / Ability Score Improvement Gain the universal Feat / Ability Score Improvement. Level 5 — Extra Attack, Improved Resolve and Relentless Challenge Attack twice when taking the Attack action. Maximum Resolve becomes 4 and Guard Die becomes d8. Relentless Challenge can maintain your current Challenge at the start of your turn without a Bonus Action when its range, perception, and Incapacitation conditions are met. Level 6 — Guardian’s Shelter and Specialization Decision / Advancement Continue your current Specialization or reassign under the universal rule, then gain the chosen path’s Level 6 advancement. Specialization Level 6 Advancement Bulwark Shared Resolve Justicar Punishing Rebuke Aegis Unyielding Ground Guardian’s Shelter: when another creature you can see within 5 ft makes a save, use your Reaction before the roll to add your CON modifier, minimum +1. If this changes failure to success, Protect the Vulnerable triggers. Bulwark — Shared Resolve: once per round, a redirected Intercession hit may spend 1 Resolve to use Resolute Guard even if already used that turn; one damage instance benefits only once. Justicar — Punishing Rebuke: a hit from Retributive Challenge sets the creature’s Speed to 0 until the end of the current turn. Aegis — Unyielding Ground: when a hostile within 5 ft willingly moves farther from you, reduce its Speed by 10 ft until end of turn, once per creature per turn; forced movement never triggers it. Level 7 — Universal Character Advancement The PHB v3.10 Templar class progression does not list a new Templar-specific feature at this level. Apply the universal Level 7 advancement normally. Level 8 — Feat / Ability Score Improvement Gain the universal Feat / Ability Score Improvement. Level 9 — Greater Resolve and Steadfast Resolve Maximum Resolve becomes 5 and Guard Die becomes d10. When you roll Initiative for a genuine combat encounter, begin with 1 Resolve instead of 0. Level 10 — Commanding Challenge and Specialization Decision / Advancement Continue your current Specialization or reassign under the universal rule, then gain the chosen path’s Level 10 advancement. Specialization Level 10 Advancement Bulwark No One Falls Justicar Judgment of Defiance Aegis Impassable Line Empyrean Bulwark — Ultimate Ability Ultimate Activation — 100 DP. As your Action and Bonus Action, make one Ultimate melee weapon attack against a creature within your reach. After the attempt resolves, enter Ultimate Recovery during your next turn. Judgment Damage. On a hit, the attack deals normal weapon damage plus fixed Radiant damage: 80 at Levels 10–14, 100 at Levels 15–19, or 120 at Level 20. Empyrean Bulwark. On a hit, choose yourself and up to PB allies within 20 ft. Each gains Resistance to all damage and cannot be moved against its will until the start of your next turn. Radius becomes 30 ft at Level 15. At Level 20, each chosen creature also gains temporary HP equal to your Templar level. Commanding Challenge: Challenge up to two visible hostiles within 30 ft and maintain up to two simultaneously. Relentless Challenge can maintain both when each qualifies. Bulwark — No One Falls: once per round, if an in-range ally is hit and the damage would reduce it to 0 HP, use Guardian’s Intercession immediately before damage even if your Reaction was already used; afterward Intercession is unavailable until your next turn. Justicar — Judgment of Defiance: Retributive Challenge hits deal one additional current Guard Die; Punishing Rebuke continues. Aegis — Impassable Line: a hostile provokes an OA when it moves 5 ft or more while within your reach, even without leaving it; once per creature per turn, and Disengage prevents it. Level 11 — Unbreakable Resolve Whenever Resolute Guard reduces damage, choose one: Stand Firm grants Advantage until your next turn on checks and saves to resist Grappled, Prone, or forced movement; Reposition lets you move 5 ft without provoking; Press the Threat makes your next melee hit against the source before the end of your next turn deal one additional Guard Die, usable once on each of your turns. Level 12 — Feat / Ability Score Improvement Gain the universal Feat / Ability Score Improvement. Level 13 — Guardian’s Rally As a Bonus Action, spend 1 Resolve and choose yourself or an ally within 10 ft. Roll your current Guard Die; the creature gains temporary HP equal to the result + CON modifier until the start of your next turn. Guardian’s Rally does not itself generate Resolve or trigger Protect the Vulnerable when those temporary HP absorb damage. text: Loot Procedure Secure the area. Identify obvious possessions and scene loot. Search for hidden items only when there is a meaningful possibility of something concealed. Recover items into personal inventory or appropriate external storage. Players distribute recovered goods by agreement. Apply quest, faction, or story rewards separately. There are no universal random loot tables. Enemies drop only what they actually possess. Equipment keeps its real quality. Fired ammunition cannot be recovered; unused ammunition can be looted. Common gear can serve as replacement gear, storage stock, sale goods, or an Aether-enhancement base. Aether gear is not a random generic drop but can be recovered from an NPC who actually owned it. Ordinary Wings are usually cosmetic loot unless explicitly mechanical. Kinah has no per-enemy formula. Unused consumables are lootable when actually present. Refined Aether is usually gathered from sources but already-refined caches are strategic loot.

text: Loot, Rewards, Missions & Selling Player Rules Exploration & Interaction Vision, stealth, traps, locks, theft, hazards, social rules, chases, and loot. Website rules source: Wings of Atreia Player Handbook v3.10 — Publication Master, 8 September 2026. This page preserves the handbook's player-facing rules and terminology. Vision, Stealth, Traps, Locks & Theft Vision and Light Cover, Line of Sight & Line of Effect Stealth and Infiltration Traps and Non-Aether Hazards Locks Theft and Pickpocket Social Interaction, Information & Captivity Vision, Stealth, Traps, Locks & Theft Vision and Light Light states are Bright Light, Dim Light, and Darkness. Obscuration states are Lightly Obscured and Heavily Obscured. Dim Light lightly obscures; Darkness heavily obscures a creature that cannot otherwise see through it. Daeva Darkvision treats Darkness within 60 feet as Dim Light, not Bright Light. A recommended ordinary light source has a stated Bright radius plus an equal additional Dim radius unless its own text says otherwise. Bright light does not universally prohibit Stealth. Obscurity and Invisibility do not automatically make a creature Hidden. Cover, Line of Sight & Line of Effect No Cover. No defensive benefit from Cover. Half Cover. A creature or object behind meaningful partial obstruction gains +2 AC and +2 to Dexterity saving throws against effects originating from the covered direction. Intervening creatures can provide Half Cover when they materially obstruct the line. Full Cover. Full Cover blocks the relevant Line of Effect and prevents direct targeting through that obstruction unless an explicit rule says otherwise. Three-Quarters Cover does not exist in Wings of Atreia. Cover does not stack; use the best applicable Cover. Altitude neither inherently grants nor ignores Cover. Line of Sight and Line of Effect are distinct. Line of Sight determines whether you can see a target or point. Line of Effect determines whether an attack, spell, or effect can physically reach it. Heavy obscurement is not Cover by itself. Stealth and Infiltration Use scene states Undetected, Suspicious, and Alerted; these are not Conditions. Stealth must exceed Passive Perception; ties favor the observer. An active Search uses the GM-selected check, commonly Wisdom (Perception) or Intelligence (Investigation), against the relevant DC or opposing Stealth; ties favor the Searcher where opposed. Do not reroll Stealth every 5 feet; roll again only when circumstances materially change. For group Stealth, at least half the group must succeed. A failed check may create Suspicion rather than immediate full alarm when appropriate. Distractions create an opportunity to Hide rather than automatic success. Disguises are primarily social. Invisibility is not the same as Hidden. Wings do not automatically prevent Stealth. Traps and Non-Aether Hazards Describe a hazard with Trigger, Detection, Avoid/Disable method, Save/Check, Effect, and Reset/Duration. Hazards may be obvious, concealed, or hidden. Detection normally uses Passive Perception, active Perception, or Investigation. Disable methods depend on the mechanism and can use Sleight of Hand, Investigation, Athletics, or another appropriate Skill. There is no mandatory Thieves’ Tools system. Failure triggers the hazard only when the hazard says so. Damage and Conditions use existing universal rules. Forced movement is horizontal unless the hazard explicitly creates vertical displacement. Hazards normally resolve when triggered rather than taking their own Initiative turns. Repeat attempts require changed circumstances. Locks Mechanical Lock DC Simple 10 Standard 12 Secure 15 High Security 18 Exceptional 20+ The correct key opens a normal lock without a check. Mechanical locks generally use Dexterity (Sleight of Hand). Unusual mechanisms can use Intelligence (Investigation). Forcing uses Strength (Athletics); destroying a lock or door uses normal object/destruction adjudication. Failure does not automatically break or trigger a lock unless its design says so. Aether locks use Aether Interaction. If a task is impossible, do not assign an absurd DC—state that it cannot be done by that method. Theft and Pickpocket A theft attempt requires a plausible opportunity. Taking an accessible small item uses Dexterity (Sleight of Hand) against Passive Perception and must exceed it. If the target is actively watching, oppose with active Perception; ties favor the observer. Secured items can require a different approach. Failure may create suspicion or alarm. Success means the theft was unnoticed at that moment; later discovery remains possible. Distraction creates opportunity rather than automatic success. Help can grant +2 when genuinely meaningful. Worn armor, shields, Wings, wielded weapons, and equipped mandatory implements cannot simply be pickpocketed. Repeated attempts require changed circumstances. Social Interaction, Information & Captivity Attitudes NPC attitudes are Friendly, Neutral, or Hostile. Roleplay comes first; a roll is used only when outcome and consequence are uncertain. Common skills include Persuasion, Deception, Intimidation, Insight, and Investigation. Plausibility A social check cannot force an impossible concession or make an NPC believe something fundamentally implausible without exceptional circumstances. Leverage affects what is possible and can influence DCs, but it does not automatically grant Advantage. Interrogation An interrogated NPC can reveal only information they actually know. Resolve one meaningful line of questioning at a time. Failure may close that approach, create resistance, or produce consequences; repeated checks need changed circumstances. Insight is not mind reading. Deception may oppose Insight when appropriate. Intimidation can succeed while still creating later consequences. Information Gathering Information comes from plausible sources. Common knowledge needs no roll. Use the skill that matches the approach. Rumors may be Reliable, Uncertain, or False, but the GM does not label them for the players. Independent sources and evidence can verify claims. Restricted information requires access. There is no fixed universal gathering-time formula and no check spam. Captivity and Restraints Physical restraints use Restrained when their actual effect warrants it. Binding an unwilling conscious creature in combat requires control first and normally an Action. Escape can use Sleight of Hand, Athletics, or Acrobatics against the restraint’s DC. A locked cell does not automatically impose Restrained. Restrained does not inherently prevent spellcasting, but implement and action requirements still matter. Ordinary restraints do not suppress Wings, Aetheric Reconstitution, or class powers unless an explicit specialized restraint says so. Transporting prisoners uses ordinary logistics. Interrogation remains a separate social procedure. Chases, Morale, Escorts & Creature Transport Chases Band Approximate Separation Engaged Immedi

text: Lower Abyss The Lower Abyss occupies the portion of Reshanta nearer Elysea, a vast aerial theater of floating landmasses separated by open voids. Terminon is the enduring Elyos staging base and a crucial point of support for operations in the region. Fortresses and routes beyond that permanent bridgehead can change hands as the campaign develops, so the military map is never completely static. Flight is fundamental here because enormous gaps make ordinary ground travel insufficient. For Daevas, the Lower Abyss turns aerial movement into strategy: patrol routes, escorts, fortress approaches, reconnaissance, and control of safe staging areas all matter. Elyos and Asmodian forces contest the wider Abyss while Balaur remain an active third power, ensuring that no simple two-sided front explains every battle. A mission can shift from open-air travel to fortress warfare or desperate rescue with little warning. The Lower Abyss is one of the clearest places where Wings of Atreia’s flight and Warfront identity becomes part of the world itself.

text: Meaningful Support and Divine Grace Maximum Divine Grace equals PB + WIS modifier, minimum 2. Long Rest restores all; Short Rest restores PB. Once per round, when you Meaningfully Support yourself or an ally with a Cleric spell or feature, regain 1 Grace. Your normal once-per-round generation becomes available again at the start of your turn, allowing an off-turn protection to qualify without double-dipping around initiative boundaries. Meaningful Support means one of the following actually occurs: restore HP while the creature was below half maximum HP; prevent or reduce damage by at least PB; or suppress/remove a mechanically significant hostile condition or effect. Healing a full-HP creature, preventing 0 damage, refreshing temporary HP without increasing it, cosmetic effects, or intentionally manufactured harmless damage do not qualify. Self-support must satisfy the same standard. Temporary HP are not healing and cannot restore a creature from 0 HP. Passive aura bonuses and passive AC do not generate Divine Grace unless a feature explicitly says so. A secondary Cleric rider created by another Cleric feature does not recursively trigger Twin Devotion, Sacred Intervention, Graceful Channeling, Empowered Restoration, or another support sequence unless explicit. Only one Cleric rolled-healing class rider normally modifies the same individual healing instance, except Graceful Restoration may coexist with one specialization rolled-healing rider. Flat Cleric save penalties do not stack; use the largest.

text: Merchant What Is a Merchant?. A Merchant has substantial experience with trade, markets, supply, negotiation, or commercial relationships. Shopkeepers, brokers, traveling traders, caravaners, suppliers, and members of merchant families can all fit this Background. Life and Origins. Trade teaches that Kinah is only part of commerce. The landscape carries scars from major conflicts, and portions of Morheim have b
text: Morheim Morheim is a mountainous and highly varied region, with sharp changes in terrain that make travel and local conditions unpredictable. Its identity is one of adaptability and defiance: communities and travelers learn quickly that one part of the region cannot stand for the whole. The landscape carries scars from major conflicts, and portions of Morheim have been profoundly altered by supernatural cold. Even so, the region remains more than the disasters that have struck it. Daevas in Morheim may move between mountain routes, settlements, damaged territory, and areas where old conflicts continue to shape present danger. Exploration and military operations can demand flexibility because terrain, weather, and strategic conditions change across the region. Stories here can focus on communities refusing to abandon difficult ground, as well as on the recovery of routes and places transformed by war. Morheim rewards characters who can adapt rather than assume every problem has the same solution.

text: Movement, Positioning & Physical Interaction Player Rules Combat Turn structure, actions, movement, attacks, damage, conditions, death, rests, and survival. Website rules source: Wings of Atreia Player Handbook v3.10 — Publication Master, 8 September 2026. This page preserves the handbook's player-facing rules and terminology. Turn Structure & Actions Genuine Combat Initiative Round and Turn Action Economy Attack Action Universal Actions Ready Turn Structure & Actions Genuine Combat Initiative, rounds, and combat-only resources are used only for genuine combat or another situation where structured turn order is necessary. Characters cannot manufacture artificial combat to farm cooldowns, resources, or timing triggers. Initiative Initiative = 1d20 + Dexterity modifier. Do not add PB unless an explicit feature says so. Alert adds +2 Initiative. There is no Surprise Round and Surprise does not grant Advantage on Initiative. When one side genuinely catches another side unaware, the GM may, at discretion, allow one appropriate pre-Initiative attack roll against the target's normal defense before Initiative is rolled. This is not an extra round, is not automatic, and does not create a general Surprise action economy. After that resolution, roll Initiative normally. Round and Turn One combat round represents approximately six seconds in the game world. Each participant normally takes one turn in Initiative order. All turns in the round abstract actions occurring within the same six-second span; do not add each turn as another six seconds. Action Economy Action. One per turn. Movement. Up to the creature’s available movement, subject to terrain and conditions. Bonus Action. Up to one, but only when a feature grants something that uses a Bonus Action. Reaction. Normally one per round, refreshing at the start of the creature’s turn unless an explicit class rule says otherwise. Object interaction. One free simple object interaction per turn. There is no universal Action-to-Bonus-Action or Bonus-Action-to-Action conversion. Unused movement or Actions are not stored for later turns. Attack Action The Attack Action makes one attack unless a feature such as Extra Attack says otherwise. Grapple and Shove are full Actions and do not replace one attack within Extra Attack. Player Weapon Requirement. A player character must be wielding an approved class weapon to take the normal Attack Action. Unarmed Attacks and Improvised Weapons are not player combat options unless a later explicit feature creates a specific exception. Opportunity Attacks. Opportunity Attacks remain part of the core combat rules. When a hostile creature you can perceive voluntarily leaves your melee reach, you may use your Reaction to make one melee attack against it, resolving the attack before it leaves that reach. Forced movement does not provoke Opportunity Attacks unless an explicit rule says otherwise. Universal Actions Dash. Gain additional movement equal to your current Speed for the turn. Difficult Terrain and other movement costs still apply. While flying, Dash adds horizontal movement but does not grant an additional altitude-layer change. Disengage. Until the end of your turn, your movement does not provoke Opportunity Attacks. Dodge. Until the start of your next turn, attacks against you have Disadvantage if you can perceive the attacker, and you have Advantage on Dexterity saving throws. Dodge ends if you become Incapacitated or your Speed becomes 0. Hide. You must have meaningful concealment or another circumstance that allows hiding. Make Dexterity (Stealth) against Passive Perception or active Perception as appropriate. You cannot Hide while clearly seen. Hidden is not Invisible. Making an attack reveals your position after that attack resolves. Search. Deliberately search using a GM-selected check, commonly Wisdom (Perception) or Intelligence (Investigation). Use Object. Use this Action for substantial manipulation beyond the one free simple object interaction. A specific item’s activation rule controls when it states another cost. Ready A creature can prepare one Action for a perceivable trigger. When the trigger occurs, the creature may use its Reaction to perform the readied Action. Ready does not store ordinary movement, but Dash can be readied as the Action. Readied attacks retain all weapon properties. A readied spell must still meet implement and targeting requirements when released. Losing a mandatory implement before release prevents release. Concentration begins when the spell actually resolves. Ready never bypasses aerial restrictions, range, or other universal rules. Simultaneous Effects Effects resolve one at a time. The active creature orders its own simultaneous effects; the GM orders GM-controlled simultaneous effects. For opposing same-time effects, resolve the active creature first, then use Initiative if needed. Damage resolves before state changes caused by that damage. Start-of-turn and end-of-turn timing is literal. Reactions follow their trigger wording and are not inserted retroactively after the consequence has already resolved unless a rule explicitly allows it. Movement, Positioning & Physical Interaction Ground Movement Base Walk. 30 feet for a Daeva unless modified. Difficult Terrain. Costs 2 feet of movement for every 1 foot traveled. Prone. Standing from Prone requires one full Action and does not consume movement. A creature can move normally afterward if movement remains available. No universal Flanking. Opposite sides do not automatically grant Advantage. No universal Facing. Being behind a creature does not automatically grant Advantage. Occupied Spaces. A creature may move through a willing allied creature's space, treating that space as difficult terrain unless an explicit feature says otherwise. A creature cannot move through an enemy or neutral creature's occupied space unless an explicit rule permits it, and cannot end movement in another creature's occupied space unless an explicit rule allows it. Grapple and Shove Grapple and Shove each require a full Action. The target must be within reach and no more than one Size larger than you. Make Strength (Athletics) contested by the target’s choice of Strength (Athletics) or Dexterity (Acrobatics). On a successful Grapple, the target becomes Grappled; it may use its Action to escape by repeating the contest. Moving a Grappled creature costs 2 feet of movement for every 1 foot moved unless the target is at least two Sizes smaller than you. On a successful Shove, choose to push the target 5 feet or knock it Prone. Grapple and Shove do not replace attacks within the Attack Action and cannot substitute for Extra Attack. Player Weapon Requirement. Player characters do not use a universal Unarmed Attack damage rule; the normal Attack Action requires an approved class weapon unless an explicit feature says otherwise. text: Noble What Is a Noble?. A Noble was raised within a household or social circle possessing wealth, prestige, distinguished ancestry, political connections, or significant influence. Life and Origins. Noble life can involve etiquette, education, reputation, family expectations, household duties, rivalries, political arrangements, and the pressure of representing more than oneself. Motivations and Outlook. A Noble may seek to serve a family, escape its expectations, restore a reputation, establish an independent legacy, protect a household, or prove that personal worth is greater than inherited status. Playing a Noble. Decide whether you embrace, reject, exploit, or feel uncomfortable with your upbringing. Noble origin describes where you came from, not how you must behave.

text: Norsvold Norsvold is a recognized Asmodian region associated with sacred memory and the deeper historical identity of the northern people. It remains part of the WoA Gazetteer while sitting outside the first-wave continental atlas, so detailed map production is intentionally deferred. Its significance lies in places where history, belief, and the Asmodian experience of survival intersect. The region should be developed from WoA canon rather than treated as a requirement to reproduce later source-story outcomes. For player characters, Norsvold can support journeys involving sacred sites, historical evidence, old obligations, and disagreements over how the past should guide the present. Religious authorities, historians, soldiers, and local communities may all approach the same places with different priorities. Adventures can explore memory without declaring every inherited belief objectively correct. Like Iluma, Norsvold remains open enough for the campaign’s discoveries to shape its future rather than merely reenacting a predetermined storyline.

Combat-capable allies roll Initiative; identical minor allies may share an Initiative when convenient. Simple verbal directions are free; complicated battlefield instructions may require an Action. Minor NPCs make Death Saves only when their survival is important to the story. NPC allies do not alter milestone advancement or create XP.

title: Open Abyss Battles
desc: Player Rules Legions & Complete Abyss Warfront System Player-created Legions plus the complete player-operable Warfront rules, unit catalogue, War Asset costs, Fortress procedures, and Open Abyss procedures. Website rules source: Wings of Atreia Core Rulebook v4.2 — Publication Master, 8 September 2026 , synchronized with Player Handbook v3.10 . This page ex
text: Open Abyss Battles Player Rules Legions & Complete Abyss Warfront System Player-created Legions plus the complete player-operable Warfront rules, unit catalogue, War Asset costs, Fortress procedures, and Open Abyss procedures. Website rules source: Wings of Atreia Core Rulebook v4.2 — Publication Master, 8 September 2026 , synchronized with Player Handbook v3.10 . This page exposes the complete player-operable Warfront subsystem. Explicitly GM-facing enemy statblocks, hidden force composition, and closed GM-only resolution tables remain off the public player site. Legions Warfront Overview War Assets Unit Statistics Battle Exchange Unit Catalogue Unit Costs PC Participation Fortress Wars Open Abyss Reinforcements Quick Reference PLAYER-CREATED LEGIONS A player-created Legion is a lightweight organization for shared identity, missions, resources, and cross-faction cooperation when the campaign permits it. Legion membership does not create a new character progression track or grant automatic combat bonuses. When a Legion Can Be Founded Campaign Gate. The Campaign Director or controlling GM must explicitly declare Legion Founding available. Reaching Level 11 by itself does not unlock the system. Founding Player. One Founding Player must be Level 11 or higher. That character becomes the initial Legion Leader. Other members. Every other founding or joining member must be Level 3 or higher before joining and must already have reached their Specialization or Archetype choice where applicable. A Level 1-2 character cannot join early. Membership has no maximum size. There is no minimum number of additional founders; a qualifying Founding Player may establish the Legion alone if all other founding requirements are satisfied. Elyos and Asmodians may belong to the same Legion once the required campaign state is active. Every member retains their original faction identity and its normal consequences. Founding Fund and Treasury Founding requires 5,000 Kinah deposited into the new Legion Treasury. Eligible founding members may contribute toward the total. Before establishment, the Founding Fund cannot be withdrawn. If founding is abandoned, each contributor receives their contribution back. Once established, the 5,000 Kinah remains usable Treasury money. Any Legion member may deposit Kinah. Only the Legion Leader may withdraw Kinah or authorize spending. Legion missions may reward participating members, the Treasury, or both as determined by the GM. There is no passive Legion income, automatic salary, interest, business-profit engine, or mandatory recurring membership dues. Leadership and Membership The only default roles are Legion Leader and Legion Member. The Legion Leader admits and removes members, controls permissions for Legion assets, may transfer leadership, and may formally dissolve the Legion. Leadership may be transferred to any existing legal Legion member. The new Leader does not need to be Level 11; Level 11 is a founding requirement only. Member Benefits Members may display the Legion name, colors, crest, and insignia. Ordinary Legion identification occupies no Inventory Slot. Members may accept Legion missions and may use resources, facilities, contacts, and support the Legion actually possesses when the Legion Leader permits it. Where the campaign's cross-faction arrangements recognize the Legion, its insignia provides a legitimate reason for Elyos and Asmodian members to operate together. It does not grant diplomatic immunity or unrestricted access. Legion membership grants no automatic Hit, AC, damage, HP, saving throw, skill, Advantage, Spell DC, DP, class-resource, equipment-quality, or personal Inventory bonus. Legion Storage and Headquarters An established Legion has one secure shared Storage location with a capacity of 100 Inventory Slots. Normal Inventory Slot and stacking rules apply; Kinah remains in the Treasury and uses no Storage Slots. Any Legion member may deposit eligible items. Only the Legion Leader may withdraw items or authorize another member to retrieve them. Legion Storage is stationary and cannot be accessed remotely. It never increases a member's personal Inventory capacity in the field. A Legion may designate one legitimate location as its Headquarters. The Headquarters is simply its meeting place and Storage location; it grants no automatic bonuses and has no upgrade track. Lightweight Rule. There is no Legion XP, Legion Level, officer hierarchy, skill tree, research tree, reputation meter, headquarters progression, or other default Legion management subsystem. Abyss Warfront System Warfronts resolve formation-scale warfare separately from ordinary character-scale combat. They are used for Fortress Wars and Open Abyss Battles. Strategic travel and marching between major engagements are handled narratively, off-table, or during downtime. Shared Warfront Command The player side uses one shared strategic board. Players collectively decide how to delegate Battlefronts or grids and who rolls the relevant Warfront dice. A player's PC location and that player's responsibility for rolling a different Battlefront are separate. Universal Synchronized Warfront Cycle Simultaneous Movement Phase. Both sides complete legal strategic movement in the same Movement Phase. Where opposing adjacent forces could advance directly into one another, the player side has advance-declaration priority. Battle Phase. Identify every engagement created by that movement. Every active engagement resolves completely, including all Battle Exchanges and Decision Windows. No Early New Movement. A Battlefront or grid that resolves early cannot begin a new normal strategic move while another engagement from that Battle Phase is unresolved. End-of-Battle-Phase Resolution. After all engagements conclude, resolve applicable control changes, recovery for eligible withdrawn Units, eliminations, retreats, and any External Reinforcement Check that is due. Then begin the next Movement Phase. No Zone of Control. Enemy adjacency by itself never locks movement. An engagement begins only when opposing forces legally enter or share the same Battlefront or grid. War Assets (WA) War Assets represent personnel, equipment, authorization, logistics, transportation, Aether resources, supplies, and the sustained resources needed to field formations. The GM declares a separate Base WA allowance for each participating side before force selection and deployment. The GM may restrict available Unit Catalogue options, Tiers, or Specialist formations for a specific operation. There is no recurring Warfront Upkeep. Unused operation-specific Base or Supplemental WA is not banked, transferred, or refunded. Only the player-controlled side may buy Supplemental WA with Kinah. title: Oriel

text: Oriel Oriel is the cultivated residential sanctuary directly beneath Sanctum on the same greater floating geography, not a distant island of its own. Gardens, estates, homes, workshops, and carefully maintained public spaces give it a gentler character than the monumental capital overhead. It reflects the domestic side of Elyos civilization: households, artistry, hospitality, and the patient work of maintaining a beautiful place to live. Its closeness to Sanctum ties everyday life directly to the political and religious heart of Elysea. Daevas who come to Oriel encounter the lives that continue beyond military service—families, artisans, residents, visitors, and generations shaped by an immortal society. The region can host social stories, community problems, personal obligations, celebrations, quiet investigations, and consequences that feel very different from fortress warfare. Its tranquility should not make it meaningless; Oriel helps show players what Elyos characters are actually protecting. Looking upward toward Sanctum also reinforces the intimate relationship between capital and home.

title: Outlander
desc: What Is an Outlander?. An Outlander has spent much of life beyond major population centers, among frontier settlements, wilderness regions, isolated communities, or people who travel far from established roads. text: Outlander What Is an Outlander?. An Outlander has spent much of life beyond major population centers, among frontier settlements, wilderness regions, isolated communities, or people who travel far from established roads. Life and Origins. Hunters, trackers, guides, scouts, wanderers, remote settlers, and similar people learn to treat terrain, weather, wildlife, supplies, and isolation as ordinary concerns. Motivations and Outlook. An Outlander may adventure from wanderlust, duty to a remote home, curiosity about the wider world, a search for someone or something, or a desire to protect places others overlook. Playing an Outlander. Consider where you feel most at home and how you react to crowded cities or unfamiliar institutions. An Outlander need not be antisocial; the Background describes experience, not personality.

title: Pandaemonium
desc: Pandaemonium is the monumental capital of Asmodae, a great center of government, military organization, scholarship, religion, trade, and culture beneath the northern darkness. It is a functioning city rather than a fortress pretending to be one, with institutions and households that reflect centuries of Asmodian reconstruction. Pernon occupies the southern
text: Pandaemonium Pandaemonium is the monumental capital of Asmodae, a great center of government, military organization, scholarship, religion, trade, and culture beneath the northern darkness. It is a functioning city rather than a fortress pretending to be one, with institutions and households that reflect centuries of Asmodian reconstruction. Pernon occupies the southern portion of the same island and serves as the capital’s cultivated residential counterpart. The city embodies the Asmodian conviction that civilization can flourish in a world shaped by hardship. Archons and other Daevas may come to Pandaemonium for orders, research, hearings, ceremonies, trade, institutional disputes, or the consequences of victories won elsewhere. Restricted military and sacred spaces coexist with ordinary civic life, giving the GM room for intrigue without making every visit a crisis. The capital should display craftsmanship, warmth, discipline, and beauty adapted to perpetual night rather than treating darkness as corruption. Pandaemonium is where Asmodae turns endurance into culture, law, memory, and ambition.

text: Pernon Pernon is the cultivated residential counterpart to Pandaemonium, occupying the southern portion of the same island rather than existing as a distant independent landmass. Homes, gardens, workshops, gathering places, and carefully maintained spaces show a quieter expression of Asmodian life. Its beauty is adapted to darkness, emphasizing shelter, craft, community, and the visual character of the northern realm. The region gives domestic life a place beside the monumental institutions of the capital. For Daevas, Pernon can make centuries of Asmodian history personal through households, neighbors, artisans, celebrations, and obligations that persist between campaigns. Adventures here may involve community concerns, social investigation, family ties, or consequences carried home from the front. It is also an important reminder that Asmodians do not exist only as soldiers in an endless war. Pernon shows what endurance is meant to preserve: a life worth returning to.

title: Player FAQ
desc: Player-safe Wings of Atreia FAQ covering the rules most likely to be misread or confused with other d20 games.
text: Player FAQ A player-safe reference for Wings of Atreia rules that are easy to misread by habit or commonly need clarification at the table. Authority. The FAQ explains the rules; it does not replace them. When a FAQ answer and the current governing rule differ, use the current Player Handbook/Core Rulebook and later explicitly approved synchronized rulings. This website version incorporates the current Ultimate miss procedure and the approved Spell Advancement clarification. Character Combat Spellcasting DP & Ultimates Flight Equipment Warfronts Classes Character Creation & Advancement Do I choose a race or species? No. Every standard player character is a Daeva . Choose Elyos or Asmodian as faction/culture. The two factions use the same universal Daeva mechanical foundation. How do I assign Ability Scores? Assign 16, 14, 14, 12, 10, and 8 freely among STR, DEX, CON, INT, WIS, and CHA. There is no ability-score rolling or point buy. Can I multiclass? No. A Daeva advances in one class from Level 1 through Level 20. Do characters gain XP? No. Advancement is Milestone only . The GM awards levels for meaningful campaign progress. When do I choose an ASI or Feat? Universal ASI/Feat choices occur at Levels 4, 8, 12, and 16 . Level 19 grants an Empyrean Boon , not another normal ASI/Feat choice. What does a Background give me? A Background gives exactly two Skill Proficiencies chosen from that Background's eligible skill list and can establish narrative relevance or permission where appropriate. It does not automatically grant Advantage, Expertise, or guaranteed success. Does duplicate proficiency become Expertise? No. Proficiency adds PB once. Expertise exists only when an explicit feature grants it. Can I change my Specialization after choosing it? Yes, but only at the normal reassignment checkpoints. Choose your initial Specialization at Level 3 . When gaining Level 6, Level 10, and Level 14 , you may either continue your current Specialization or switch to another Specialization available to your class. The Level 14 decision is the final normal Specialization choice through Level 20. If I switch Specializations, do I keep features from my old path? No. Remove every feature granted by the previous Specialization and replace it with the new Specialization's complete feature package through the current checkpoint. Features from different paths cannot be mixed or retained. Make any choices required by newly gained features, and remove, reselect, or recalculate path-dependent options, capacities, and maxima as necessary. Reassignment itself restores no HP or class resources, and current values cannot remain above a new maximum. Can I change Specialization during downtime or by training? No. Normal reassignment happens only while gaining Level 6, 10, or 14. Rest, downtime, training, ordinary retraining, or time between adventures does not create an extra reassignment opportunity. d20 Tests, Actions & Combat Are natural 1 and natural 20 automatic on every d20 Test? No. Ability Checks and Saving Throws compare the final total to the DC. Attack rolls keep their explicit natural-1 automatic miss and natural-20 automatic hit/critical rules. How does Help work? A meaningful helper gives +2 to one Ability Check . Help does not grant Advantage. There is no Assist Attack, and Help does not modify Death Saves. Can Grapple or Shove replace one attack from Extra Attack? No. Grapple and Shove are each a full Action . How do I stand from Prone? Standing from Prone requires your full Action and consumes no movement. Does flanking automatically grant Advantage? No. Wings of Atreia has no universal Flanking rule and no universal Facing rule. Is there a Surprise Round? No. In a genuine ambush, the GM may allow one appropriate pre-Initiative attack. That is discretionary and is not an extra round. How is 3D distance measured? When horizontal and vertical separation both matter, use the greater of the two distances rather than adding them. Does taking damage at 0 HP automatically add failed Death Saves? No. Ordinary damage while already at 0 HP does not alter the Death Save track. A natural 1 on a Death Save is exactly one failure. Spellcasting Does Wings of Atreia use spell slots or cantrips? No. There are no spell slots and no cantrip category. Each spell has its own frequency: At-Will, Cooldown, Short Rest, or Long Rest. Does ordinary damage force a Concentration save? No. Ordinary damage does not test Concentration. Concentration ends only according to the Wings of Atreia Concentration rules and explicit effects. Can I buy, copy, or learn spells from scrolls? Not as a universal rule. Spells are class-granted and unlock through class progression and their printed prerequisites. Does every Spell Advancement make the spell mechanically stronger? No. One Spell Advancement raises one eligible unlocked spell by exactly +1 Spell Level . A Spell Level is not automatically a mechanical improvement breakpoint. If the new Spell Level is not listed in that spell's Spell-Level Scaling or Milestone Improvements , record the higher Spell Level normally but do not change damage, healing, range, area, duration, riders, or any other effect. Do not invent compensation. The progression-only Spell Level remains valid permanent progression, may satisfy prerequisites, and counts toward the next listed improvement. Can I skip an unexciting Spell Level and jump to the next improvement? No. Each Spell Advancement increases the selected eligible spell by exactly one Spell Level. Progression-only levels are still real levels. Does casting a Bonus Action spell prevent me from casting another spell that turn? No universal D&D-style Bonus Action spell restriction exists. Follow the actual Action/Bonus Action timing and the individual spell text. Daeva Points & Ultimates When do I gain Daeva Points and unlock my Ultimate? Beginning at Level 10 , eligible Daevas can earn DP from genuine combat. Maximum DP is 100. At 100 DP, the class Ultimate is ready. Does only the character who lands the killing blow gain DP? No. Eligible Level 10+ Daevas who meaningfully participated receive the full qualifying post-combat DP award; it is not divided by killing blows. What happens when my Ultimate attack misses? After the miss is confirmed, the player chooses one of two final resolutions: Release the Power: spend all 100 DP and resolve one-half, rounded down, of the Ultimate's fixed primary damage plus one-half of any direct Ultimate healing, restoration, or repair amount that would have occurred on a hit. Normal weapon/Bastion damage, area or secondary-target damage, temporary HP/protection, forced movement, conditions/status effects, condition removal, and other riders do not occur. There is no next-dawn lockout . Hold the Power: resolve no Ultimate effect, retain all 100 DP, and that Ultimate cannot be attempted again until the next dawn. Rests and Aetheric Reconstitution do not end the lockout early. Ultimate Recovery occurs after eit

title: Player Quick Reference
desc: Character creation, level-up, actions, conditions, feats, boons, flight, inventory, Aether enhancement, and class-resource quick tables.
text: Player Quick Reference Character creation, level-up, actions, conditions, feats, boons, flight, inventory, Aether enhancement, and class-resource quick tables. Source: Wings of Atreia Player Handbook v3.10 — Publication Master, 8 September 2026. This page is a player-facing reference extracted from the handbook rather than a replacement ruleset. Character Creation Level Up Actions Conditions Feats Boons Flight Inventory Aether Enhancement Class Resources Appendix A — Character Creation Checklist □ Choose Elyos or Asmodian. □ Choose one of the 11 classes. □ Assign 16, 14, 14, 12, 10, 8 among STR, DEX, CON, INT, WIS and CHA. □ Choose one Background. □ Record class saving throws, armor, shield and weapon access. □ Choose class skills and two Background skills. □ Calculate HP, AC, Initiative, class Save DC, Speed and Passive Perception. □ Record the fixed class starting weapon/implement, armor, Common Wings, and starting Kinah (500 + 250 per level above 1). □ Choose name, appearance, wing appearance, personality, history, relationships and motivation. Appendix B — Level-Up Checklist Specialization Reassignment: Choose the initial path at Level 3. When gaining Levels 6, 10, and 14, either continue that path or switch to another class Specialization. Switching removes the previous path's entire feature package and replaces it with the new path's complete package through the current checkpoint. Recalculate path-dependent choices and maxima as required; reassignment restores no HP or resources. Level 14 is the final normal choice. □ Read the full new class-level entry and specialization text. □ Apply fixed HP gain + CON + class durability. □ Update PB if needed. □ Update class resource caps/dice/ranges/chassis. □ Make ASI/Feat choice if granted. □ Choose Empyrean Boon at Level 19. □ Apply Spell Advancements if granted. □ Update Flight Slots, Exploration Flight and Inventory. □ Recalculate DCs, spell attacks, AC and passive values. □ At Level 10, add the Daeva Point tracker and class Ultimate; use the improved values at Levels 15 and 20. Appendix C — Universal Action Reference Action Cost What It Does Attack Action Make one attack unless Extra Attack or an explicit feature changes the number. Dash Action Gain additional movement equal to current Speed for the turn; movement costs still apply. While flying, no extra altitude-layer change. Disengage Action Until end of your turn, your movement does not provoke Opportunity Attacks. Dodge Action Until start of your next turn, attacks against you have Disadvantage if you perceive the attacker; you have Advantage on DEX saves. Ends if Incapacitated or Speed 0. Help Action +2 to one meaningful Ability Check; no Advantage; cannot Assist Attack or Death Saves. Hide Action Require meaningful concealment; DEX (Stealth) vs Passive/active Perception. Cannot Hide while clearly seen. Hidden is not Invisible; an attack reveals position after it resolves. Ready Action + later Reaction Prepare one Action for a perceivable trigger; release with Reaction. Search Action when structured timing matters Use the GM-selected check, commonly WIS (Perception) or INT (Investigation), against the relevant DC or Stealth. Use Object Action when substantial manipulation is required Substantial manipulation beyond the free simple object interaction; a specific item’s activation rule controls if it states another cost. Grapple Action Full Action; target in reach and no more than one Size larger; STR (Athletics) vs target STR (Athletics) or DEX (Acrobatics). Escape uses Action. Dragging normally costs 2:1. Shove Action Full Action; same contest and Size/reach limits as Grapple. On success push 5 ft or knock Prone. Stand from Prone Action Full Action; does not consume movement. Equip / Remove Shield Action Full Action. Appendix D — Conditions Fourteen universal Conditions: Blinded, Charmed, Deafened, Frightened, Grappled, Incapacitated, Invisible, Paralyzed, Petrified, Poisoned, Prone, Restrained, Stunned, Unconscious. Hidden is not a Condition. Condition Player-Facing Effect Blinded A Blinded creature cannot see and automatically fails Ability Checks that require sight. Attack rolls against it have Advantage, and its attack rolls have Disadvantage. It can still move normally unless another rule limits its movement, and Blinded does not inherently cause an airborne creature to fall. Charmed A Charmed creature cannot willingly attack, damage, or directly target its charmer with a harmful ability or effect. The charmer has Advantage on appropriate social Ability Checks directed at the Charmed creature. Charmed is not total mind control: it does not create automatic obedience, betrayal, disclosure of secrets, or suicidal behavior. Deafened A Deafened creature cannot hear and automatically fails Ability Checks that require hearing. Deafened creates no generic combat penalty by itself, but the creature cannot benefit from an effect that explicitly requires it to hear the source unless that effect says otherwise. Frightened While the source of its fear is within Line of Sight, a Frightened creature has Disadvantage on Ability Checks and attack rolls and cannot willingly move closer to that source. Frightened imposes no general saving-throw penalty. An airborne Frightened creature may remain airborne and may move sideways or away from the source subject to normal flight rules. Grappled A Grappled creature’s Speed becomes 0. The condition ends if the grappler becomes Incapacitated, the target is moved outside the grappler’s reach, or an explicit effect ends the Grapple. The Grappled creature may use its Action to attempt the approved escape contest. Grappled does not inherently cause Prone or falling; airborne movement follows the normal grappling and forced-movement rules. Incapacitated An Incapacitated creature cannot take Actions, Bonus Actions, or Reactions and cannot maintain Concentration. Incapacitated does not itself reduce Speed to 0, cause Prone, or cause an airborne creature to fall. Invisible An Invisible creature cannot normally be seen without a special sense or revealing effect. Attack rolls against it have Disadvantage and its attack rolls have Advantage when the opposing creature cannot otherwise perceive it, subject to the normal unseen-attacker and unseen-target rules. Invisible is not automatically Hidden; sound, footprints, disturbances, and other evidence can still reveal its location. Paralyzed A Paralyzed creature is Incapacitated, its Speed is 0, and it cannot move or speak. It automatically fails Strength and Dexterity saving throws, and attack rolls against it have Advantage. Paralyzed does not cause automatic Critical Hits. If unsupported, the creature becomes Prone; an unsupported airborne Paralyzed creature therefore falls. Petrified A Petrified creature and its carried nonmagical equipment are transformed into inert solid substance. text: Poeta Poeta is a fertile rural region of Elysea, defined by broad plains, farms, forests, and clear lakes. Akarios Village stands among a landscape that includes Cliona Lake, Daminu Forest, Kabarah Strip Mine, and Timolia Mine. Compared with the grandeur of Sanctum, Poeta feels close to the land and to the ordinary rhythms of food, work, family, and local community. Its pastoral appearance makes it one of the clearest expressions of the hospitable southern environment. For many Elyos, Poeta represents homeland in its most immediate form: fields worth tending, communities worth defending, and wilderness that still holds mysteries of its own. Daevas may be called to protect travelers, investigate trouble around mines and forests, assist isolated settlements, or deal with dangers that ordinary residents cannot face alone. The region works especially well for adventures where local stakes matter before the campaign expands into larger wars. Poeta reminds heroes that the fate of Atreia is ultimately measured in the lives that survive its conflicts.

title: Ranger
desc: Complete player reference for the Ranger class in Wings of Atreia, based on Player Handbook v3.10.
text: Ranged Striker • Focus • Traps • Tactical Repositioning Ranger “Chase me or run away. Either way, you'll only die tired.” Website rules source: Wings of Atreia Player Handbook v3.10 — Publication Master, 8 September 2026. This page preserves the handbook's class material and ordering. Class Identity Class Chassis Core Engine — Focus Resource Flow — Generation, Recovery, Spending & Reset Specializations Preview Level 1–20 Action & Resource Reference Level-by-Level Progression Example Combat Sequences Specialization Reassignment The Ranger is a nonmagical ranged hunter that controls enemy movement with persistent battlefield traps, spends Focus on precision or evasive shots, and is rewarded for exploiting targets that walk into prepared terrain. Its sustained damage comes from two ranged attacks, not from spellcasting or a third standard attack. Class Identity Rangers are mobile ranged specialists who control distance through marksmanship, movement, traps, and battlefield awareness. They are most effective when they can read terrain before committing, choose favorable lines of attack, and punish enemies that approach carelessly. Focus represents the Ranger’s ability to convert patience and perception into precise action. Tradition & Outlook The Ranger tradition also descends from Atreia’s scout disciplines, but where Assassins close with a chosen target, Rangers cultivate distance, fieldcraft, and control of the approach. Rangers are common among scouts, hunters, pathfinders, border wardens, reconnaissance troops, and independent Daevas accustomed to surviving beyond secure settlements. They tend to value preparedness, observation, mobility, and freedom of movement. Appearance & Adventuring Rangers usually wear mobile armor and carry bows, ammunition, traps, and field equipment suited to extended movement. Their gear often reflects the terrain in which they learned their craft. Rangers adventure to explore dangerous regions, hunt monsters or enemy operatives, guide expeditions, secure routes, protect remote communities, or prove that no battlefield is truly open ground when preparation and range are on their side. A Long Rest restores all expended Focus. A Short Rest restores Focus equal to PB, up to your maximum. Focus is a tactical reserve rather than ammunition or a tax on ordinary ranged attacks; Ranger Traps normally cost no Focus. Resource Flow — Generation, Recovery, Spending & Reset Resource Flow Rule Starting State Focus is a rest-based reserve and does not reset merely because combat begins or ends. After a Long Rest it is normally full. Maximum PB + WIS modifier, minimum 2. Rest Recovery Long Rest restores all expended Focus. Short Rest restores Focus equal to PB, up to your maximum. Combat Recovery Hunter’s Rhythm and certain later Ranger/specialization features can regain Focus during genuine combat when their tactical conditions are actually satisfied. How You Spend It Precision Shot 1 Focus; Pinning Shot 1 Focus; Evasive Step 1 Focus; Deadeye Perfect Shot 1 Focus. Other Ranger features spend Focus only when their text states a cost. Refunds / Recovery A combat refund or recovery is not a new attack, trap trigger, or separate technique. It simply restores Focus up to your maximum. Persistence Unused Focus persists between encounters until spent or restored; there is no automatic combat-end reset. Does Not Generate Standing still and firing, harmless staged interactions, or ordinary trap placement do not create Focus unless an explicit recovery feature is actually triggered. text: Required Implements and Components Sorcerer. Must have an equipped Magical Orb or Spellbook. Spiritmaster. Must have an equipped Magical Orb or Spellbook. Songweaver. Must have an equipped Lute or Lyre. Cleric. No mandatory casting implement. Chanter. No mandatory casting implement. Narrative speech, gestures, music, prayer, or Aetheric movements may describe casting but are not universal mechanical components. Merely being unable to speak or hear does not automatically prevent casting. There are no universal component pouches, reagent costs, gemstones, Refined Aether costs, or Kinah costs unless the particular effect explicitly says so. Required Implement Loss. A required implement must be equipped and usable according to its hand requirement; merely carrying it is insufficient. Losing, dropping, stowing, being disarmed of, or otherwise unequipping a required implement prevents only new spells and class features that require that implement until an appropriate implement is equipped again. It does not disable the rest of the class, automatically end a spell already successfully cast, or automatically dismiss an already-summoned Spirit unless the specific spell or class feature explicitly requires continued implement use.

text: Reshanta / The Abyss Reshanta is the immense physical space between Elysea and Asmodae. Floating landmasses, fortresses, Tower remnants, and vast open gaps make flight central to travel and warfare throughout the Abyss. Lower Abyss The Lower Abyss occupies the portion of Reshanta nearer Elysea, a vast aerial theater of floating landmasses separated by open voids. Terminon is the enduring Elyos staging base and a crucial point of support for operations in the region. Fortresses and routes beyond that permanent bridgehead can change hands as the campaign develops, so the military map is never completely static. Flight is fundamental here because enormous gaps make ordinary ground travel insufficient. For Daevas, the Lower Abyss turns aerial movement into strategy: patrol routes, escorts, fortress approaches, reconnaissance, and control of safe staging areas all matter. Elyos and Asmodian forces contest the wider Abyss while Balaur remain an active third power, ensuring that no simple two-sided front explains every battle. A mission can shift from open-air travel to fortress warfare or desperate rescue with little warning. The Lower Abyss is one of the clearest places where Wings of Atreia’s flight and Warfront identity becomes part of the world itself. Upper Abyss The Upper Abyss lies nearer Asmodae and shares the shattered aerial geography that defines Reshanta. Primum is the enduring Asmodian staging base, providing a lasting foothold amid territory whose other fortresses may change control through the campaign. Floating islands, fortress positions, open gaps, and exposed flight paths make geography inseparable from military planning. The region is physical space within Atreia, not another dimension. Archons and other Daevas operating here must think in three dimensions, because height, approach routes, airborne interception, and the security of landing points can determine whether a mission succeeds. Elyos rivals and Balaur forces can both threaten an operation, while changing fortress control continually reshapes local priorities. The Upper Abyss supports patrols, raids, rescues, reconnaissance, and full Warfront engagements without requiring every encounter to become a mass battle. Its proximity to Asmodae makes the centuries-long Abyss War feel immediate to northern characters. Core / Eye of Reshanta The Core, also called the Eye of Reshanta, occupies the central strategic heart of the Abyss between Elysea and Asmodae. It is the most symbolically and militarily charged part of Reshanta, centered on the Divine Fortress and the central Balaur order that holds the starting-era position. Tower remnants and the immense broken interior of Atreia dominate the surrounding sense of scale. Reaching the Core means moving toward the center of a war that has endured for centuries. Neither Elyos nor Asmodians can treat the Core as ordinary homeland territory, and operations here carry consequences far beyond a single patrol. Balaur power, fortress strategy, aerial approaches, and the ambitions of both Daeva factions converge around the Eye. Player actions may eventually change the balance, because the starting map establishes a beginning rather than a protected future. The Core should feel like a place where tactical success can become history.

text: Resource Flow — Generation, Recovery, Spending & Reset Resource Flow Rule Resource Form Rune Marks are target-bound counters, not a generic personal pool.
