Failure triggers the hazard only when the hazard says so. Damage and Conditions use existing universal rules. Forced movement is horizontal unless the hazard explicitly creates vertical displacement. Hazards normally resolve when triggered rather than taking their own Initiative turns. Repeat attempts require changed circumstances.

title: Turn Structure & Actions
desc: Player Rules Combat Turn structure, actions, movement, attacks, damage, conditions, death, rests, and survival. Website rules source: Wings of Atreia Player Handbook v3.10 — Publication Master, 8 September 2026. This page preserves the handbook's player-facing rules and terminology. Turn Structure & Actions Genuine Combat Initiative Round and Turn Action Eco
text: Turn Structure & Actions Player Rules Combat Turn structure, actions, movement, attacks, damage, conditions, death, rests, and survival. Website rules source: Wings of Atreia Player Handbook v3.10 — Publication Master, 8 September 2026. This page preserves the handbook's player-facing rules and terminology. Turn Structure & Actions Genuine Combat Initiative Round and Turn Action Economy Attack Action Universal Actions Ready Turn Structure & Actions Genuine Combat Initiative, rounds, and combat-only resources are used only for genuine combat or another situation where structured turn order is necessary. Characters cannot manufacture artificial combat to farm cooldowns, resources, or timing triggers. Initiative Initiative = 1d20 + Dexterity modifier. Do not add PB unless an explicit feature says so. Alert adds +2 Initiative. There is no Surprise Round and Surprise does not grant Advantage on Initiative. When one side genuinely catches another side unaware, the GM may, at discretion, allow one appropriate pre-Initiative attack roll against the target's normal defense before Initiative is rolled. This is not an extra round, is not automatic, and does not create a general Surprise action economy. After that resolution, roll Initiative normally. Round and Turn One combat round represents approximately six seconds in the game world. Each participant normally takes one turn in Initiative order. All turns in the round abstract actions occurring within the same six-second span; do not add each turn as another six seconds. Action Economy Action. One per turn. Movement. Up to the creature’s available movement, subject to terrain and conditions. Bonus Action. Up to one, but only when a feature grants something that uses a Bonus Action. Reaction. Normally one per round, refreshing at the start of the creature’s turn unless an explicit class rule says otherwise. Object interaction. One free simple object interaction per turn. There is no universal Action-to-Bonus-Action or Bonus-Action-to-Action conversion. Unused movement or Actions are not stored for later turns. Attack Action The Attack Action makes one attack unless a feature such as Extra Attack says otherwise. Grapple and Shove are full Actions and do not replace one attack within Extra Attack. Player Weapon Requirement. A player character must be wielding an approved class weapon to take the normal Attack Action. Unarmed Attacks and Improvised Weapons are not player combat options unless a later explicit feature creates a specific exception. Opportunity Attacks. Opportunity Attacks remain part of the core combat rules. When a hostile creature you can perceive voluntarily leaves your melee reach, you may use your Reaction to make one melee attack against it, resolving the attack before it leaves that reach. Forced movement does not provoke Opportunity Attacks unless an explicit rule says otherwise. Universal Actions Dash. Gain additional movement equal to your current Speed for the turn. Difficult Terrain and other movement costs still apply. While flying, Dash adds horizontal movement but does not grant an additional altitude-layer change. Disengage. Until the end of your turn, your movement does not provoke Opportunity Attacks. Dodge. Until the start of your next turn, attacks against you have Disadvantage if you can perceive the attacker, and you have Advantage on Dexterity saving throws. Dodge ends if you become Incapacitated or your Speed becomes 0. Hide. You must have meaningful concealment or another circumstance that allows hiding. Make Dexterity (Stealth) against Passive Perception or active Perception as appropriate. You cannot Hide while clearly seen. Hidden is not Invisible. Making an attack reveals your position after that attack resolves. Search. Deliberately search using a GM-selected check, commonly Wisdom (Perception) or Intelligence (Investigation). Use Object. Use this Action for substantial manipulation beyond the one free simple object interaction. A specific item’s activation rule controls when it states another cost. Ready A creature can prepare one Action for a perceivable trigger. When the trigger occurs, the creature may use its Reaction to perform the readied Action. Ready does not store ordinary movement, but Dash can be readied as the Action. Readied attacks retain all weapon properties. A readied spell must still meet implement and targeting requirements when released. Losing a mandatory implement before release prevents release. Concentration begins when the spell actually resolves. Ready never bypasses aerial restrictions, range, or other universal rules. Simultaneous Effects Effects resolve one at a time. The active creature orders its own simultaneous effects; the GM orders GM-controlled simultaneous effects. For opposing same-time effects, resolve the active creature first, then use Initiative if needed. Damage resolves before state changes caused by that damage. Start-of-turn and end-of-turn timing is literal. Reactions follow their trigger wording and are not inserted retroactively after the consequence has already resolved unless a rule explicitly allows it. Movement, Positioning & Physical Interaction Ground Movement Base Walk. 30 feet for a Daeva unless modified. Difficult Terrain. Costs 2 feet of movement for every 1 foot traveled. Prone. Standing from Prone requires one full Action and does not consume movement. A creature can move normally afterward if movement remains available. No universal Flanking. Opposite sides do not automatically grant Advantage. No universal Facing. Being behind a creature does not automatically grant Advantage. Occupied Spaces. A creature may move through a willing allied creature's space, treating that space as difficult terrain unless an explicit feature says otherwise. A creature cannot move through an enemy or neutral creature's occupied space unless an explicit rule permits it, and cannot end movement in another creature's occupied space unless an explicit rule allows it. Grapple and Shove Grapple and Shove each require a full Action. The target must be within reach and no more than one Size larger than you. Make Strength (Athletics) contested by the target’s choice of Strength (Athletics) or Dexterity (Acrobatics). On a successful Grapple, the target becomes Grappled; it may use its Action to escape by repeating the contest. Moving a Grappled creature costs 2 feet of movement for every 1 foot moved unless the target is at least two Sizes smaller than you. On a successful Shove, choose to push the target 5 feet or knock it Prone. Grapple and Shove do not replace attacks within the Attack Action and cannot substitute for Extra Attack. Player Weapon Requirement. Player characters do not use a universal Unarmed Attack damage rule; the normal Attack Action requires an approved class weapon unless an explicit feature says otherwise. Disarm Disarm is a full Action. The attacker uses Strength (Athletics) or Dexterity (Sleight of Hand), contested by the defende

title: Understanding Your Background
desc: Your Class describes what your character has learned to do as an adventuring Daeva. Your Background describes the life, training, profession, upbringing, or experiences that helped shape who they were before the campaign began. Faction tells you where you belong, Background helps explain where you came from, and Class describes how you operate as an adventur
text: Understanding Your Background Your Class describes what your character has learned to do as an adventuring Daeva. Your Background describes the life, training, profession, upbringing, or experiences that helped shape who they were before the campaign began. Faction tells you where you belong, Background helps explain where you came from, and Class describes how you operate as an adventurer. A Background does not determine your morality, personality, beliefs, faction loyalty, or future choices. Two characters with the same Background may have completely different lives and goals. Mechanically, use the Background table above exactly as written: choose two skills from your Background’s listed skill pool. The entries below add roleplaying context and do not grant additional rules benefits.

title: Underworld

text: Underworld What Is the Underworld?. Here, Underworld means the hidden networks of crime, illicit commerce, secrecy, unofficial influence, and socially marginal activity beneath respectable society. It does not mean a supernatural realm of the dead. Life and Origins. The character may have lived or worked among thieves, smugglers, fences, informants, lookouts, infiltrators, fixers, or others who survive through clandestine networks. They may also have entered such circles while working against them. Motivations and Outlook. Money, survival, freedom from former associates, revenge, protection, redemption, influence, or unfinished debts may draw the character onward. Playing an Underworld Character. Decide whether you left that life, remain connected to it, or were never truly a criminal at all. This Background does not require evil behavior or continuing criminal activity.

text: Universal Actions Dash. Gain additional movement equal to your current Speed for the turn. Difficult Terrain and other movement costs still apply. While flying, Dash adds horizontal movement but does not grant an additional altitude-layer change. Disengage. Until the end of your turn, your movement does not provoke Opportunity Attacks. Dodge. Until the start of your next turn, attacks against you have Disadvantage if you can perceive the attacker, and you have Advantage on Dexterity saving throws. Dodge ends if you become Incapacitated or your Speed becomes 0. Hide. You must have meaningful concealment or another circumstance that allows hiding. Make Dexterity (Stealth) against Passive Perception or active Perception as appropriate. You cannot Hide while clearly seen. Hidden is not Invisible. Making an attack reveals your position after that attack resolves. Search. Deliberately search using a GM-selected check, commonly Wisdom (Perception) or Intelligence (Investigation). Use Object. Use this Action for substantial manipulation beyond the one free simple object interaction. A specific item’s activation rule controls when it states another cost.

text: Universal Gunslinger Safeguards A secondary Gunslinger effect produced by Tempo gain, Tempo refund, ammunition restoration, movement, specialization riders, or technique riders does not recursively trigger another Gunslinger rider unless explicitly stated. Flat Gunslinger class-feature penalties to the same statistic do not stack unless explicitly stated; use the largest. text: Universal Gunslinger Techniques Technique Cost Exact Level 1 Effect Quick Shot 1 Tempo Cost: 1 Tempo. Once on each of your turns after making a firearm attack with a Pistol, make one additional Pistol attack as a Bonus Action. Quick Shot consumes ammunition normally, cannot generate Tempo, cannot be used with a Musket, and cannot trigger another Quick Shot. Deliberate Shot 1 Tempo Once on each of your turns when a Musket hit resolves, add +1d8 weapon damage to that hit. Not another attack; expends no additional ammunition; cannot generate Tempo; the added die is part of the attack for critical hits. Evasive Shot 1 Tempo Cost: 1 Tempo. Reaction when a hostile creature you can see makes an attack roll against you. Before the attack resolves, move 5 feet without provoking from that creature. If that movement makes you an illegal target for the triggering attack, the attack misses; otherwise it resolves normally. You must be able to move. Evasive Shot does not trigger against area effects. Disrupting Shot 1 Tempo Cost: 1 Tempo. When a firearm attack hits, choose one effect for that attack: Hamstring (Speed -10 feet until the start of your next turn), Break Aim (-1 to the creature's next attack roll before your next turn), or Drive Back (push 5 feet if the target is no more than one size larger). Specializations — Read Before You Choose Gunslinger chooses an initial Specialization at Level 3. Use this preview before reading the Level 1–20 progression so you can see the playstyle each path develops into. Specialization features are gained at Levels 3, 6, 10, and 14. Specialization Preview Specialization Identity What You Can Expect Pistolero Rapid dual-pistol pressure Emphasizes twin-gun rhythm, fast draws, barrages, and sustained Tempo-driven shooting. Best for players who want aggressive, stylish, high-volume firearm turns. Deadeye Precision marksman Improves careful shots, critical windows, positioning, piercing fire, and execution accuracy. Best for players who want fewer but more deliberate high-value shots. Saboteur Technical ammunition and disruption Uses modified ammunition and specialized payloads to interfere with enemies and recover through disruption. Best for players who enjoy tactical riders and control through firearm technology. Specialization Advancement Preview Level Pistolero Deadeye Saboteur 3 Twin Gun Rhythm; Rapid Draw Precision Window; Steady Sight Modified Ammunition; Technical Ballistics 6 Crossfire; Tempo Barrage Critical Focus; Precision Reposition Specialized Payload; Disruption Recovery 10 Bullet Dance; Relentless Barrage Piercing Shot; Lethal Calibration Disabling Round; Improved Disruption Recovery 14 Grand Barrage; Perfect Akimbo Execution Window; Perfect Sight Grand Sabotage; Feeding Disruption Specialization Reassignment Initial choice — Level 3. Choose one Specialization available to your class. Reassignment checkpoints — Levels 6, 10, and 14. When gaining one of these levels, you may either continue your current Specialization or change to another Specialization available to your class. If you change Specialization, remove every feature granted by the previous Specialization and replace it with the complete feature package of the newly selected Specialization through your current checkpoint . Features from different Specializations cannot be mixed, retained, or combined. When newly entering a Specialization, make any choices required by the features you now gain. Continuing the same Specialization does not reset earlier internal choices unless an explicit feature says otherwise. If the removed Specialization granted extra known options, selections, capacities, or Specialization-dependent maxima, remove, reselect, or recalculate them as necessary to satisfy the new path. Reassignment itself does not restore HP or class resources, and current values cannot remain above any new maximum. Reassignment occurs only as part of gaining Level 6, Level 10, or Level 14 . It cannot be performed through a rest, downtime, training, ordinary retraining, or between adventures. The Level 14 decision is the final normal Specialization choice and remains locked through Level 20 unless a later explicit rule says otherwise.

text: Universal Spellcasting Player Rules Aether & Spellcasting Aether environment and interaction, universal spellcasting, and Spell Advancement. Website rules source: Wings of Atreia Player Handbook v3.10 — Publication Master, 8 September 2026. This page preserves the handbook's player-facing rules and terminology. Aether Environment, Interaction & Gathering Aether Interaction Aether Sources Refined Aether Gathering Aether Hazards Universal Spellcasting Universal Model Spell Acquisition Aether Environment, Interaction & Gathering Aether Interaction Aether Interaction uses Intelligence (Arcana) for intellectual analysis and Dexterity (Sleight of Hand) for physical manipulation. Typical DC guidance is 10, 12, 15, 18, or 20+ according to complexity and danger. Aether Sources Nodes, Currents, Fissures, and other environmental Aether phenomena can provide opportunities, hazards, travel effects, or Refined Aether. Their exact scene behavior is defined by the source. Refined Aether Gathering Gathering Refined Aether uses Dexterity (Sleight of Hand) against the source DC. Aether Level DC Yield Range Default Yield 1 8 2–6 4 2 10 6–12 9 3 12 12–24 18 4 15 24–40 32 5 18 40–60 50 The GM identifies a valid source and its Aether Level. Only the interacting character rolls. Apply normal modifiers and Help only if actually meaningful. On success, gain a yield within the listed range based on source richness; if no special richness is established, use the Default Yield. A successful gathering normally exhausts that source. Multiple deposits exist only when the GM explicitly establishes them. Failure gives no Refined Aether and does not automatically exhaust the source, but a new attempt requires a meaningful change in circumstances. Another party member does not automatically create a fresh attempt. Normal gathering is not performed during active combat unless gathering itself is an explicit encounter objective. Already-refined Aether recovered from caches or stores is ordinary loot and requires no gathering check. Aether Hazards Aether Hazards use the universal sequence Trigger → Save → DC → Effect → Duration. Standard severity bands are Minor DC 10–11, Moderate DC 12–14, Severe DC 15–17, and Extreme DC 18–20+. The four approved hazard families are Aether Storm, Aether Surge, Aether Eruption, and Unstable Zone. Each specific hazard defines its actual Trigger, Save, Effect, and Duration. Dangerous Aether changes are normally telegraphed in advance unless the hazard is specifically concealed. Strategic Refined Aether uses not defined in this handbook are deferred unless a future subsystem explicitly establishes them. Vehicle-related Refined Aether rules remain deferred with vehicle rules, and the current Abyss Warfront system uses no universal Refined Aether conversion for Fortress power. Universal Spellcasting Universal Model WoA has no spell slots and no cantrip category. Each spell is individually At-Will, Cooldown-based, Short-Rest limited, or Long-Rest limited. Class resources may modify spells but are not universal casting costs. Spell Acquisition Spells are class-granted abilities. They cannot be bought, sold, looted, copied from spellbooks or scrolls, learned from vendors, or acquired by commerce or exploration. A spell becomes available only when the character reaches its Unlock Level and, when applicable, satisfies the immediately preceding spell in its linear prerequisite chain. Unlocking a later spell never removes the earlier spell. Newly unlocked spells begin at Spell Level 1 unless explicitly stated otherwise. Spell Advancement — Final Rule. A class grants Spell Advancements according to its finalized progression. One Spell Advancement raises one eligible unlocked spell by 1 Spell Level, subject to that class’s Maximum Spell Level and listed prerequisites. Unspent Spell Advancements may be banked indefinitely, but banked or newly earned Spell Advancements may be spent only when the character gains a level; they cannot normally be spent during an adventure, between encounters, or during a rest. A character cannot spend more Spell Advancements than they have earned. Spell Retraining. There is no universal spell retraining. Once a Spell Advancement is spent, it is permanent unless a specific class feature, explicit story effect, or GM-approved exceptional circumstance directly permits reassignment. Casting Frequency and Action Economy At-Will spells may be cast whenever action economy permits. Cooldown X spells become available at the start of the caster’s Xth turn after the casting turn. Round-based cooldowns advance only during genuine combat; artificial Initiative cannot refresh, farm, or manipulate cooldowns or class resources. Outside genuine combat, a Cooldown spell becomes available again 1 minute after use unless the spell states a longer restriction. Short-Rest and Long-Rest spells regain uses after the named rest. Casting Time is binding. Casting multiple spells in one turn is allowed only when the character actually has the required Actions and no class or spell restriction forbids it. Wings of Atreia has no universal D&D bonus-action-spell restriction. Spellcasting Classes The finalized spellcasting classes are Sorcerer, Spiritmaster, Cleric, Chanter, and Songweaver. This handbook integrates the complete 106-spell library: Sorcerer 24, Spiritmaster 22, Cleric 20, Chanter 16, and Songweaver 24. Required Implements and Components Sorcerer. Must have an equipped Magical Orb or Spellbook. Spiritmaster. Must have an equipped Magical Orb or Spellbook. Songweaver. Must have an equipped Lute or Lyre. Cleric. No mandatory casting implement. Chanter. No mandatory casting implement. Narrative speech, gestures, music, prayer, or Aetheric movements may describe casting but are not universal mechanical components. Merely being unable to speak or hear does not automatically prevent casting. There are no universal component pouches, reagent costs, gemstones, Refined Aether costs, or Kinah costs unless the particular effect explicitly says so. Required Implement Loss. A required implement must be equipped and usable according to its hand requirement; merely carrying it is insufficient. Losing, dropping, stowing, being disarmed of, or otherwise unequipping a required implement prevents only new spells and class features that require that implement until an appropriate implement is equipped again. It does not disable the rest of the class, automatically end a spell already successfully cast, or automatically dismiss an already-summoned Spirit unless the specific spell or class feature explicitly requires continued implement use. Casting and Conditions A creature cannot cast if an existing Condition prevents the required Action, Bonus Action, or Reaction. Incapacitated, and therefore Stunned/Paralyzed/Unconscious when they include Incapacitated, prevents casting. text: Universal Unit Catalogue Player Rules Legions & Complete Abyss Warfront System Player-created Legions plus the complete player-operable Warfront rules, unit catalogue, War Asset costs, Fortress procedures, and Open Abyss procedures. Website rules source: Wings of Atreia Core Rulebook v4.2 — Publication Master, 8 September 2026 , synchronized with Player Handbook v3.10 . This page exposes the complete player-operable Warfront subsystem. Explicitly GM-facing enemy statblocks, hidden force composition, and closed GM-only resolution tables remain off the public player site. Legions Warfront Overview War Assets Unit Statistics Battle Exchange Unit Catalogue Unit Costs PC Participation Fortress Wars Open Abyss Reinforcements Quick Reference PLAYER-CREATED LEGIONS A player-created Legion is a lightweight organization for shared identity, missions, resources, and cross-faction cooperation when the campaign permits it. Legion membership does not create a new character progression track or grant automatic combat bonuses. When a Legion Can Be Founded Campaign Gate. The Campaign Director or controlling GM must explicitly declare Legion Founding available. Reaching Level 11 by itself does not unlock the system. Founding Player. One Founding Player must be Level 11 or higher. That character becomes the initial Legion Leader. Other members. Every other founding or joining member must be Level 3 or higher before joining and must already have reached their Specialization or Archetype choice where applicable. A Level 1-2 character cannot join early. Membership has no maximum size. There is no minimum number of additional founders; a qualifying Founding Player may establish the Legion alone if all other founding requirements are satisfied. Elyos and Asmodians may belong to the same Legion once the required campaign state is active. Every member retains their original faction identity and its normal consequences. Founding Fund and Treasury Founding requires 5,000 Kinah deposited into the new Legion Treasury. Eligible founding members may contribute toward the total. Before establishment, the Founding Fund cannot be withdrawn. If founding is abandoned, each contributor receives their contribution back. Once established, the 5,000 Kinah remains usable Treasury money. Any Legion member may deposit Kinah. Only the Legion Leader may withdraw Kinah or authorize spending. Legion missions may reward participating members, the Treasury, or both as determined by the GM. There is no passive Legion income, automatic salary, interest, business-profit engine, or mandatory recurring membership dues. Leadership and Membership The only default roles are Legion Leader and Legion Member. The Legion Leader admits and removes members, controls permissions for Legion assets, may transfer leadership, and may formally dissolve the Legion. Leadership may be transferred to any existing legal Legion member. The new Leader does not need to be Level 11; Level 11 is a founding requirement only. Member Benefits Members may display the Legion name, colors, crest, and insignia. Ordinary Legion identification occupies no Inventory Slot. Members may accept Legion missions and may use resources, facilities, contacts, and support the Legion actually possesses when the Legion Leader permits it. Where the campaign's cross-faction arrangements recognize the Legion, its insignia provides a legitimate reason for Elyos and Asmodian members to operate together. It does not grant diplomatic immunity or unrestricted access. Legion membership grants no automatic Hit, AC, damage, HP, saving throw, skill, Advantage, Spell DC, DP, class-resource, equipment-quality, or personal Inventory bonus. Legion Storage and Headquarters An established Legion has one secure shared Storage location with a capacity of 100 Inventory Slots. Normal Inventory Slot and stacking rules apply; Kinah remains in the Treasury and uses no Storage Slots. Any Legion member may deposit eligible items. Only the Legion Leader may withdraw items or authorize another member to retrieve them. Legion Storage is stationary and cannot be accessed remotely. It never increases a member's personal Inventory capacity in the field. A Legion may designate one legitimate location as its Headquarters. The Headquarters is simply its meeting place and Storage location; it grants no automatic bonuses and has no upgrade track. Lightweight Rule. There is no Legion XP, Legion Level, officer hierarchy, skill tree, research tree, reputation meter, headquarters progression, or other default Legion management subsystem. Abyss Warfront System Warfronts resolve formation-scale warfare separately from ordinary character-scale combat. They are used for Fortress Wars and Open Abyss Battles. Strategic travel and marching between major engagements are handled narratively, off-table, or during downtime. Shared Warfront Command The player side uses one shared strategic board. Players collectively decide how to delegate Battlefronts or grids and who rolls the relevant Warfront dice. A player's PC location and that player's responsibility for rolling a different Battlefront are separate. Universal Synchronized Warfront Cycle Simultaneous Movement Phase. Both sides complete legal strategic movement in the same Movement Phase. Where opposing adjacent forces could advance directly into one another, the player side has advance-declaration priority. Battle Phase. Identify every engagement created by that movement. Every active engagement resolves completely, including all Battle Exchanges and Decision Windows. No Early New Movement. A Battlefront or grid that resolves early cannot begin a new normal strategic move while another engagement from that Battle Phase is unresolved. End-of-Battle-Phase Resolution. After all engagements conclude, resolve applicable control changes, recovery for eligible withdrawn Units, eliminations, retreats, and any External Reinforcement Check that is due. Then begin the next Movement Phase. No Zone of Control. Enemy adjacency by itself never locks movement. An engagement begins only when opposing forces legally enter or share the same Battlefront or grid. War Assets (WA) War Assets represent personnel, equipment, authorization, logistics, transportation, Aether resources, supplies, and the sustained resources needed to field formations. The GM declares a separate Base WA allowance for each participating side before force selection and deployment. The GM may restrict available Unit Catalogue options, Tiers, or Specialist formations for a specific operation. There is no recurring Warfront Upkeep. Unused operation-specific Base or Supplemental WA is not banked, transferred, or refunded. Only the player-controlled side may buy Supplemental WA with Kinah. Recommended Baseline WA Warfront Attacker Defender Open Abyss Battle 100 WA 100 WA Standard Fortress War 150 WA 100 WA Major Fortress War 350 WA 200 WA These are recommended operational baselines, not mandatory encounter budgets. text: Upper Abyss The Upper Abyss lies nearer Asmodae and shares the shattered aerial geography that defines Reshanta. Primum is the enduring Asmodian staging base, providing a lasting foothold amid territory whose other fortresses may change control through the campaign. Floating islands, fortress positions, open gaps, and exposed flight paths make geography inseparable from military planning. The region is physical space within Atreia, not another dimension. Archons and other Daevas operating here must think in three dimensions, because height, approach routes, airborne interception, and the security of landing points can determine whether a mission succeeds. Elyos rivals and Balaur forces can both threaten an operation, while changing fortress control continually reshapes local priorities. The Upper Abyss supports patrols, raids, rescues, reconnaissance, and full Warfront engagements without requiring every encounter to become a mass battle. Its proximity to Asmodae makes the centuries-long Abyss War feel immediate to northern characters.

text: Verteron Verteron is a temperate defensive frontier where plains, coastline, woodland, roads, and old ruins meet. Verteron Citadel anchors the region alongside Tolbas Village, Verteron Observatory, Cantas Coast, Tursin Garrison, Zumion Ruins, and the road leading toward Eltnen. Its settled routes are never entirely removed from military vigilance, giving the region the feel of civilization pressed against contested ground. Ancient remains and active defenses stand side by side across the landscape. Service in Verteron emphasizes readiness, patrols, escort duty, reconnaissance, and the defense of communities that live close to danger. Daevas can move from a village problem to a ruined site or hostile position without leaving the region’s broader defensive story. The coexistence of roads, settlements, ruins, and enemy activity makes Verteron a natural place for exploration and field missions. It is a reminder that Elysea’s beauty survives partly because someone is always watching its frontiers.

Website rules source: Wings of Atreia Player Handbook v3.10 — Publication Master, 8 September 2026. This page preserves the handbook's player-facing rules and terminology. Vision, Stealth, Traps, Locks & Theft Vision and Light Cover, Line of Sight & Line of Effect Stealth and Infiltration Traps and Non-Aether Hazards Locks Theft and Pickpocket Social Interaction, Information & Captivity Vision, Stealth, Traps, Locks & Theft Vision and Light Light states are Bright Light, Dim Light, and Darkness. Obscuration states are Lightly Obscured and Heavily Obscured. Dim Light lightly obscures; Darkness heavily obscures a creature that cannot otherwise see through it. Daeva Darkvision treats Darkness within 60 feet as Dim Light, not Bright Light. A recommended ordinary light source has a stated Bright radius plus an equal additional Dim radius unless its own text says otherwise. Bright light does not universally prohibit Stealth. Obscurity and Invisibility do not automatically make a creature Hidden. Cover, Line of Sight & Line of Effect No Cover. No defensive benefit from Cover. Half Cover. A creature or object behind meaningful partial obstruction gains +2 AC and +2 to Dexterity saving throws against effects originating from the covered direction. Intervening creatures can provide Half Cover when they materially obstruct the line. Full Cover. Full Cover blocks the relevant Line of Effect and prevents direct targeting through that obstruction unless an explicit rule says otherwise. Three-Quarters Cover does not exist in Wings of Atreia. Cover does not stack; use the best applicable Cover. Altitude neither inherently grants nor ignores Cover. Line of Sight and Line of Effect are distinct. Line of Sight determines whether you can see a target or point. Line of Effect determines whether an attack, spell, or effect can physically reach it. Heavy obscurement is not Cover by itself. Stealth and Infiltration Use scene states Undetected, Suspicious, and Alerted; these are not Conditions. Stealth must exceed Passive Perception; ties favor the observer. An active Search uses the GM-selected check, commonly Wisdom (Perception) or Intelligence (Investigation), against the relevant DC or opposing Stealth; ties favor the Searcher where opposed. Do not reroll Stealth every 5 feet; roll again only when circumstances materially change. For group Stealth, at least half the group must succeed. A failed check may create Suspicion rather than immediate full alarm when appropriate. Distractions create an opportunity to Hide rather than automatic success. Disguises are primarily social. Invisibility is not the same as Hidden. Wings do not automatically prevent Stealth. Traps and Non-Aether Hazards Describe a hazard with Trigger, Detection, Avoid/Disable method, Save/Check, Effect, and Reset/Duration. Hazards may be obvious, concealed, or hidden. Detection normally uses Passive Perception, active Perception, or Investigation. Disable methods depend on the mechanism and can use Sleight of Hand, Investigation, Athletics, or another appropriate Skill. There is no mandatory Thieves’ Tools system. Failure triggers the hazard only when the hazard says so. Damage and Conditions use existing universal rules. Forced movement is horizontal unless the hazard explicitly creates vertical displacement. Hazards normally resolve when triggered rather than taking their own Initiative turns. Repeat attempts require changed circumstances. Locks Mechanical Lock DC Simple 10 Standard 12 Secure 15 High Security 18 Exceptional 20+ The correct key opens a normal lock without a check. Mechanical locks generally use Dexterity (Sleight of Hand). Unusual mechanisms can use Intelligence (Investigation). Forcing uses Strength (Athletics); destroying a lock or door uses normal object/destruction adjudication. Failure does not automatically break or trigger a lock unless its design says so. Aether locks use Aether Interaction. If a task is impossible, do not assign an absurd DC—state that it cannot be done by that method. Theft and Pickpocket A theft attempt requires a plausible opportunity. Taking an accessible small item uses Dexterity (Sleight of Hand) against Passive Perception and must exceed it. If the target is actively watching, oppose with active Perception; ties favor the observer. Secured items can require a different approach. Failure may create suspicion or alarm. Success means the theft was unnoticed at that moment; later discovery remains possible. Distraction creates opportunity rather than automatic success. Help can grant +2 when genuinely meaningful. Worn armor, shields, Wings, wielded weapons, and equipped mandatory implements cannot simply be pickpocketed. Repeated attempts require changed circumstances. Social Interaction, Information & Captivity Attitudes NPC attitudes are Friendly, Neutral, or Hostile. Roleplay comes first; a roll is used only when outcome and consequence are uncertain. Common skills include Persuasion, Deception, Intimidation, Insight, and Investigation. Plausibility A social check cannot force an impossible concession or make an NPC believe something fundamentally implausible without exceptional circumstances. Leverage affects what is possible and can influence DCs, but it does not automatically grant Advantage. Interrogation An interrogated NPC can reveal only information they actually know. Resolve one meaningful line of questioning at a time. Failure may close that approach, create resistance, or produce consequences; repeated checks need changed circumstances. Insight is not mind reading. Deception may oppose Insight when appropriate. Intimidation can succeed while still creating later consequences. Information Gathering Information comes from plausible sources. Common knowledge needs no roll. Use the skill that matches the approach. Rumors may be Reliable, Uncertain, or False, but the GM does not label them for the players. Independent sources and evidence can verify claims. Restricted information requires access. There is no fixed universal gathering-time formula and no check spam. Captivity and Restraints Physical restraints use Restrained when their actual effect warrants it. Binding an unwilling conscious creature in combat requires control first and normally an Action. Escape can use Sleight of Hand, Athletics, or Acrobatics against the restraint’s DC. A locked cell does not automatically impose Restrained. Restrained does not inherently prevent spellcasting, but implement and action requirements still matter. Ordinary restraints do not suppress Wings, Aetheric Reconstitution, or class powers unless an explicit specialized restraint says so. Transporting prisoners uses ordinary logistics. text: War Asset Price Catalogue Player Rules Legions & Complete Abyss Warfront System Player-created Legions plus the complete player-operable Warfront rules, unit catalogue, War Asset costs, Fortress procedures, and Open Abyss procedures. Website rules source: Wings of Atreia Core Rulebook v4.2 — Publication Master, 8 September 2026 , synchronized with Player Handbook v3.10 . This page exposes the complete player-operable Warfront subsystem. Explicitly GM-facing enemy statblocks, hidden force composition, and closed GM-only resolution tables remain off the public player site. Legions Warfront Overview War Assets Unit Statistics Battle Exchange Unit Catalogue Unit Costs PC Participation Fortress Wars Open Abyss Reinforcements Quick Reference PLAYER-CREATED LEGIONS A player-created Legion is a lightweight organization for shared identity, missions, resources, and cross-faction cooperation when the campaign permits it. Legion membership does not create a new character progression track or grant automatic combat bonuses. When a Legion Can Be Founded Campaign Gate. The Campaign Director or controlling GM must explicitly declare Legion Founding available. Reaching Level 11 by itself does not unlock the system. Founding Player. One Founding Player must be Level 11 or higher. That character becomes the initial Legion Leader. Other members. Every other founding or joining member must be Level 3 or higher before joining and must already have reached their Specialization or Archetype choice where applicable. A Level 1-2 character cannot join early. Membership has no maximum size. There is no minimum number of additional founders; a qualifying Founding Player may establish the Legion alone if all other founding requirements are satisfied. Elyos and Asmodians may belong to the same Legion once the required campaign state is active. Every member retains their original faction identity and its normal consequences. Founding Fund and Treasury Founding requires 5,000 Kinah deposited into the new Legion Treasury. Eligible founding members may contribute toward the total. Before establishment, the Founding Fund cannot be withdrawn. If founding is abandoned, each contributor receives their contribution back. Once established, the 5,000 Kinah remains usable Treasury money. Any Legion member may deposit Kinah. Only the Legion Leader may withdraw Kinah or authorize spending. Legion missions may reward participating members, the Treasury, or both as determined by the GM. There is no passive Legion income, automatic salary, interest, business-profit engine, or mandatory recurring membership dues. Leadership and Membership The only default roles are Legion Leader and Legion Member. The Legion Leader admits and removes members, controls permissions for Legion assets, may transfer leadership, and may formally dissolve the Legion. Leadership may be transferred to any existing legal Legion member. The new Leader does not need to be Level 11; Level 11 is a founding requirement only. Member Benefits Members may display the Legion name, colors, crest, and insignia. Ordinary Legion identification occupies no Inventory Slot. Members may accept Legion missions and may use resources, facilities, contacts, and support the Legion actually possesses when the Legion Leader permits it. Where the campaign's cross-faction arrangements recognize the Legion, its insignia provides a legitimate reason for Elyos and Asmodian members to operate together. It does not grant diplomatic immunity or unrestricted access. Legion membership grants no automatic Hit, AC, damage, HP, saving throw, skill, Advantage, Spell DC, DP, class-resource, equipment-quality, or personal Inventory bonus. Legion Storage and Headquarters An established Legion has one secure shared Storage location with a capacity of 100 Inventory Slots. Normal Inventory Slot and stacking rules apply; Kinah remains in the Treasury and uses no Storage Slots. Any Legion member may deposit eligible items. Only the Legion Leader may withdraw items or authorize another member to retrieve them. Legion Storage is stationary and cannot be accessed remotely. It never increases a member's personal Inventory capacity in the field. A Legion may designate one legitimate location as its Headquarters. The Headquarters is simply its meeting place and Storage location; it grants no automatic bonuses and has no upgrade track. Lightweight Rule. There is no Legion XP, Legion Level, officer hierarchy, skill tree, research tree, reputation meter, headquarters progression, or other default Legion management subsystem. Abyss Warfront System Warfronts resolve formation-scale warfare separately from ordinary character-scale combat. They are used for Fortress Wars and Open Abyss Battles. Strategic travel and marching between major engagements are handled narratively, off-table, or during downtime. Shared Warfront Command The player side uses one shared strategic board. Players collectively decide how to delegate Battlefronts or grids and who rolls the relevant Warfront dice. A player's PC location and that player's responsibility for rolling a different Battlefront are separate. Universal Synchronized Warfront Cycle Simultaneous Movement Phase. Both sides complete legal strategic movement in the same Movement Phase. Where opposing adjacent forces could advance directly into one another, the player side has advance-declaration priority. Battle Phase. Identify every engagement created by that movement. Every active engagement resolves completely, including all Battle Exchanges and Decision Windows. No Early New Movement. A Battlefront or grid that resolves early cannot begin a new normal strategic move while another engagement from that Battle Phase is unresolved. End-of-Battle-Phase Resolution. After all engagements conclude, resolve applicable control changes, recovery for eligible withdrawn Units, eliminations, retreats, and any External Reinforcement Check that is due. Then begin the next Movement Phase. No Zone of Control. Enemy adjacency by itself never locks movement. An engagement begins only when opposing forces legally enter or share the same Battlefront or grid. War Assets (WA) War Assets represent personnel, equipment, authorization, logistics, transportation, Aether resources, supplies, and the sustained resources needed to field formations. The GM declares a separate Base WA allowance for each participating side before force selection and deployment. The GM may restrict available Unit Catalogue options, Tiers, or Specialist formations for a specific operation. There is no recurring Warfront Upkeep. Unused operation-specific Base or Supplemental WA is not banked, transferred, or refunded. Only the player-controlled side may buy Supplemental WA with Kinah. Recommended Baseline WA Warfront Attacker Defender Open Abyss Battle 100 WA 100 WA Standard Fortress War 150 WA 100 WA Major Fortress War 350 WA 200 WA These are recommended operational baselines, not mandatory encounter budgets.

title: World of Atreia
desc: Player-safe guide to the regions of Elysea, Asmodae, Reshanta, and the known Balaurea frontier.
text: Setting Reference World of Atreia A spoiler-safe guide to the shattered world, its major realms, and the regions Daevas may know in the Present Age. History of Atreia From ancient Atreia to the opening age of the Abyss War. Elysea Sanctum, Oriel, Poeta, Verteron, Eltnen, Heiron, Theobomos, and Iluma. Asmodae Pandaemonium, Pernon, Ishalgen, Altgard, Morheim, Beluslan, Brusthonin, and Norsvold. Reshanta / The Abyss Lower Abyss, Upper Abyss, and the Core / Eye of Reshanta. Balaurea Inggison, Gelkmaros, Silentera Canyon, and the largely unknown greater frontier. Before You Explore the World Atreia was not always divided. Discover how the rise of the Balaur, the Millennium War, the Cataclysm, and the opening of the Abyss shaped the age in which your Daeva begins their story. Read the History of Atreia → Elysea Elysea forms the southern half of shattered Atreia and is the homeland of the Elyos. Its regions range from fertile countryside and monumental cities to arid badlands, mountain forests, devastated islands, and places where ancient history remains close to the surface. Sanctum Sanctum is the monumental floating capital of Elysea, suspended above Oriel and visible as one of the great symbols of Elyos civilization. Its luminous plazas, temples, government halls, Legion offices, archives, and scholarly institutions make it a center of civic life as much as military power. The city was raised during the long southern reconstruction after the Cataclysm rather than surviving unchanged from ancient Atreia. Public ceremony, learning, art, diplomacy, and service all contribute to the capital’s cultivated identity. For Elyos Daevas, Sanctum is where victories become policy, discoveries enter archives, and service to Elysea can draw the attention of powerful institutions. Most civic areas are orderly and accessible, while military compounds, temple spaces, and restricted records remain controlled. Adventures here tend toward investigation, diplomacy, political consequences, research, or threats hidden beneath the security of the capital. Sanctum represents what Elyos society believes it rebuilt from the ruin of the old world. Oriel Oriel is the cultivated residential sanctuary directly beneath Sanctum on the same greater floating geography, not a distant island of its own. Gardens, estates, homes, workshops, and carefully maintained public spaces give it a gentler character than the monumental capital overhead. It reflects the domestic side of Elyos civilization: households, artistry, hospitality, and the patient work of maintaining a beautiful place to live. Its closeness to Sanctum ties everyday life directly to the political and religious heart of Elysea. Daevas who come to Oriel encounter the lives that continue beyond military service—families, artisans, residents, visitors, and generations shaped by an immortal society. The region can host social stories, community problems, personal obligations, celebrations, quiet investigations, and consequences that feel very different from fortress warfare. Its tranquility should not make it meaningless; Oriel helps show players what Elyos characters are actually protecting. Looking upward toward Sanctum also reinforces the intimate relationship between capital and home. Poeta Poeta is a fertile rural region of Elysea, defined by broad plains, farms, forests, and clear lakes. Akarios Village stands among a landscape that includes Cliona Lake, Daminu Forest, Kabarah Strip Mine, and Timolia Mine. Compared with the grandeur of Sanctum, Poeta feels close to the land and to the ordinary rhythms of food, work, family, and local community. Its pastoral appearance makes it one of the clearest expressions of the hospitable southern environment. For many Elyos, Poeta represents homeland in its most immediate form: fields worth tending, communities worth defending, and wilderness that still holds mysteries of its own. Daevas may be called to protect travelers, investigate trouble around mines and forests, assist isolated settlements, or deal with dangers that ordinary residents cannot face alone. The region works especially well for adventures where local stakes matter before the campaign expands into larger wars. Poeta reminds heroes that the fate of Atreia is ultimately measured in the lives that survive its conflicts. Verteron Verteron is a temperate defensive frontier where plains, coastline, woodland, roads, and old ruins meet. Verteron Citadel anchors the region alongside Tolbas Village, Verteron Observatory, Cantas Coast, Tursin Garrison, Zumion Ruins, and the road leading toward Eltnen. Its settled routes are never entirely removed from military vigilance, giving the region the feel of civilization pressed against contested ground. Ancient remains and active defenses stand side by side across the landscape. Service in Verteron emphasizes readiness, patrols, escort duty, reconnaissance, and the defense of communities that live close to danger. Daevas can move from a village problem to a ruined site or hostile position without leaving the region’s broader defensive story. The coexistence of roads, settlements, ruins, and enemy activity makes Verteron a natural place for exploration and field missions. It is a reminder that Elysea’s beauty survives partly because someone is always watching its frontiers. Eltnen Eltnen is Elysea’s distinctly arid region, a landscape of dry badlands, exposed stone, scarce water, and scattered greener pockets where life gathers. Its harsher terrain contrasts sharply with Poeta’s fertility and demonstrates that the southern realm is not uniformly lush. Settlements and travelers must respect distance, water, weather, and the limits imposed by the land. Ruins and isolated routes can feel especially exposed beneath the bright Elysean sky. Life in Eltnen is shaped by adaptation rather than abundance. Daevas operating here may protect water access, cross dangerous open country, investigate remote ruins, escort travelers, or respond to threats that exploit the region’s isolation. Communities that endure here have practical knowledge of the terrain and should feel capable rather than helpless. Eltnen gives Elyos adventures a frontier defined as much by environment and distance as by warfare. Heiron Heiron is a forested and mountainous region of Elysea, rich in waterways, steep terrain, old roads, and places where wilderness can conceal history. Its dense landscapes and changes in elevation distinguish it from both arid Eltnen and rural Poeta. The region carries a strong sense of vigilance and memory, with civilization existing beside terrain that can quickly become difficult or dangerous. Water, forest, and stone shape both travel and settlement. For Daevas, Heiron favors scouting, pursuit, defense, historical investigation, and expeditions into places where the landscape can hide ruins or hostile movement. Roads and communities remain important, but control of a route does not mean control of everything beyond it. Th

title: Current Campaign Start: The Present Age
desc: Circa 1,000 AC: newly Ascended Daevas enter the Abyss War, with Elyos, Asmodians, Balaur, Terminon, Primum, Balaurea, Silentera, and Lepharist revolutionaries shaping the opening campaign.
text: Current Campaign Start: The Present Age The default Wings of Atreia campaign begins circa 1,000 AC, during the long Abyss War. Player characters begin as newly Ascended Daevas who have only recently received their Wings and entered an immortal life of service, discovery, and conflict. Elyos and Asmodians remain bitter rivals, with Terminon and Primum serving as their enduring footholds in Reshanta, while the Balaur stand as a powerful third force rather than a distant legend. Beyond the familiar realms, the known Balaurean frontier has opened through Inggison, Gelkmaros, and Silentera Canyon, but Greater Balaurea remains largely unknown. Your Daeva begins with a faction, a homeland, and reasons to distrust the opposing side, but the world does not promise that every enemy will remain simple. Early adventures can place Elyos and Asmodians against the same Balaur threat, and circumstances may force rivals to decide whether survival matters more than inherited hatred. Lepharist revolutionaries are active in this age and may become part of the characters’ first encounters with the wider conflict, but their deeper motives are something players discover through play. The starting world is therefore a snapshot, not a fixed future: fortresses can change hands, alliances can form or collapse, and the actions of player characters can become part of Atreia’s history.

title: The Twelve Empyrean Lords
desc: Ariel, Kaisinel, Nezekan, Vaizel, Yustiel, Azphel, Lumiel, Marchutan, Triniel, Zikel, Israphel, and Siel; their player-facing roles, institutions, traditions, and historical legacies.
text: The Twelve Empyrean Lords The Empyrean Lords are extraordinary Daevas elevated into Lordhood whose names stand at the heart of Atreia’s history. After the Cataclysm, the surviving rulers became associated with the Seraphim tradition of Elysea and the Shedim tradition of Asmodae, while the two Tower Guardians remain central to the story of the world’s division. To player characters, these Lords are not merely distant mythology: their institutions, teachings, military orders, laws, temples, and legacies shape the societies in which Daevas live. Seraphim Lords of Elysea Ariel — Lady of Light Kaisinel — Lord of Illusion Nezekan — Lord of Justice Vaizel — Lord of Freedom Yustiel — Lady of Life These Lords stand among the highest powers recognized in Elyos civilization. Their influence reaches player characters through Sanctum, Elyos institutions, military service, cultural traditions, and the expectations placed upon Daevas. A player may serve organizations shaped by a Lord’s legacy, receive missions from authorities acting in a Lord’s name, or eventually become important enough for the concerns of the Lords themselves to matter. Shedim Lords of Asmodae Azphel — Lord of Shadow Lumiel — Lady of Wisdom Marchutan — Lord of Fate Triniel — Lady of Death Zikel — Lord of Destruction These Lords stand among the highest powers recognized in Asmodian civilization. Their influence is felt through Pandaemonium, Archon service, Asmodian institutions, cultural traditions, and the hard-won identity of Asmodae. Player characters may encounter their authority through commanders, temples, missions, judgments, and eventually events important enough to draw the attention of the Lords themselves. The Tower Guardians Israphel — Lord of Space Siel — Lady of Time Israphel and Siel are remembered as the two Guardians of the Tower of Eternity and are counted among the Twelve Empyrean Lords of Atreia’s great history. Their roles are different from those of the post-Cataclysm faction rulers: they belong to the story of the Tower, the Cataclysm, and the sacrifice that shaped the divided world. For beginning players, their importance is primarily historical, and deeper truths concerning their legacy are meant to be discovered through the campaign rather than explained in advance.

title: The Six Dragon Lords
desc: Fregion, Meslamtaeda, Ereshkigal, Beritra, Tiamat, and Apsu; the supreme Balaur powers and their spoiler-safe roles toward player characters.
text: The Six Dragon Lords The Dragon Lords are the supreme powers of the Balaur and represent threats on a scale far beyond ordinary soldiers or monsters. Their names are known through history, warfare, rumor, and the devastation associated with Balaur dominion. Player characters are far more likely to encounter their armies, agents, fortresses, schemes, and consequences before ever standing before a Dragon Lord directly. Fregion — Dragon Lord of Fire Fregion is remembered as the first Dragon Lord and the beginning of the transformation that produced the Balaur order. To players, his name represents the oldest and greatest shadow behind Balaur power. Any direct involvement with Fregion belongs to the highest scale of Daeva conflict rather than ordinary adventuring. Meslamtaeda — Dragon Lord of Rage and Destruction Meslamtaeda embodies overwhelming destructive power among the Dragon Lords. Players should understand his influence through the fear, devastation, and military consequences associated with forces acting beneath such a ruler. Confronting power of this magnitude is not the same as facing a conventional battlefield commander. Ereshkigal — Dragon Lord of Ice and Justice Ereshkigal is one of the great Balaur powers whose name is bound to the long struggle surrounding the Abyss. For players, she represents a strategic power capable of shaping entire theaters of war rather than merely individual encounters. Her deeper circumstances in the Present Age are intentionally left for discovery during play. Beritra — Dragon Lord of Darkness Beritra is a Dragon Lord whose power extends through Balaur forces, plans, and conflicts reaching beyond any single region. Player characters may experience that influence through enemies and events long before understanding the full design behind them. His true objectives and present movements are matters for the campaign to reveal. Tiamat — Dragon Lord of Earth and Death Tiamat commands power associated with conquest, warfare, and Balaur dominion. To beginning Daevas, her name belongs to the class of enemies capable of moving armies and changing the fate of territories. What she seeks in the Present Age—and how her struggles with other Balaur powers affect Atreia—should emerge through play. Apsu — Dragon Lord of Wind Apsu is counted among the Six Dragon Lords and remains part of the history and power structure players inherit at the start of the campaign. Public knowledge does not provide beginning characters with a complete account of his present circumstances. His deeper role is therefore deliberately left unexplained here so that the campaign can reveal it at the proper time. What the Lords mean to your character: Empyrean Lords can stand behind the institutions, duties, beliefs, and authorities that shape a Daeva’s life, while Dragon Lords define the scale of the Balaur threat looming over both factions. Neither group should be reduced to a list of quest-givers or boss fights. As the campaign grows, the players’ relationship to these powers can change from distant history and military consequence to direct choices capable of affecting Atreia itself.
